For several days now she has been simply in a kind of fever, and she has already drawn up a whole plan for how, later on, you can be Pyotr Petrovich’s associate and even partner in his legal business, all the more since you are in the law faculty yourself. I, Rodya, entirely agree with her and share all her plans and hopes, seeing every likelihood in them; and, in spite of Pyotr Petrovich’s present reserve, which is very understandable (because he does not know you yet), Dunya is firmly convinced that she will achieve everything by her good influence on her future husband, and of this she is sure. Of course we have taken care not to let slip a word to Pyotr Petrovich about any of these further dreams of ours, and above all that you will be his partner. He is a practical man and might take it very coldly, since all this would seem to him nothing but dreams. In the same way, neither Dunya nor I have said half a word to him yet about our strong hope that he will help us to help you with money while you are at the university; we have not said it because, first, it will come about of itself later, and he will surely offer it himself without unnecessary words (as if he would refuse Dunechka that), all the sooner since you yourself can become his right hand in the office and receive this help not as a charity but as a salary you have earned. That is how Dunechka wants to arrange it, and I entirely agree with her. And secondly, we have not said it because I particularly wanted to put you on an equal footing with him at our coming meeting. When Dunya spoke to him about you with enthusiasm, he answered that one must first look at any man oneself and more closely before judging him, and that he reserves the right to form his own opinion of you when he has made your acquaintance. Do you know, my precious Rodya, it seems to me, for certain reasons (not in the least to do with Pyotr Petrovich, though, but just for certain of my own personal, perhaps even old-womanish, womanish whims), it seems to me that I shall perhaps do better to live on my own after their marriage, as I live now, and not with them. I am quite sure that he will be so noble and delicate that he will invite me himself and offer that I should not be parted from my daughter any more, and if he has not said so yet, it is of course because it is understood without words; but I shall refuse. I have noticed more than once in life that mothers-in-law are not much to husbands’ liking, and I not only do not want to be the slightest burden to anyone, but I want to be completely free myself, as long as I have some bit of my own and such children as you and Dunechka. If possible I shall settle near you both, because, Rodya, I have saved the nicest thing for the end of the letter: know, my dear friend, that perhaps very soon we shall all come together again and embrace, all three of us, after a separation of almost three years! It is already settled for certain that Dunya and I are setting off for Petersburg; exactly when, I do not know, but in any case very, very soon, perhaps even in a week. Everything depends on the arrangements of Pyotr Petrovich, who will let us know as soon as he has looked about him in Petersburg. For certain reasons of his own he wants to hasten the marriage ceremony as much as possible, and even, if possible, to have the wedding during the present meat-eating season, and if that cannot be managed, because the time is so short, then immediately after the Assumption fast. Oh, with what happiness I shall press you to my heart! Dunya is all excited with joy at seeing you, and she said once, as a joke, that she would have married Pyotr Petrovich for that alone. She is an angel! She is not adding anything to this letter now, but only told me to write that she has so much, so much to talk to you about, that she cannot bring herself to take up her pen now, because one can write nothing in a few lines and only upset oneself; but she told me to give you a tight hug and send you countless kisses. But although we may perhaps meet in person very soon, I shall still send you some money in a day or two, as much as I can. Now that everyone knows that Dunechka is marrying Pyotr Petrovich, my credit has suddenly grown too, and I know for certain that Afanasy Ivanovich will now trust me, against my pension, even up to seventy-five roubles, so that I may perhaps send you twenty-five roubles or even thirty. I would send more, but I am afraid for our travelling expenses; and although Pyotr Petrovich has been so kind as to take on part of the expenses of our journey to the capital, namely, he has offered of his own accord, at his own expense, to send our luggage and the big trunk (somehow through acquaintances of his), still we have to reckon on our arrival in Petersburg, where one cannot appear without a penny, at least for the first days. Dunechka and I, however, have already worked it all out exactly, and it turned out that the journey will not cost much. It is only ninety versts from us to the railway, and we have already, just in case, arranged with a peasant driver we know; and from there Dunechka and I will ride very comfortably third class. So that perhaps I shall manage to send you not twenty-five but surely thirty roubles. But enough; I have filled two sheets all round, and there is no more room; our whole story; well, and so many things have happened! And now, my precious Rodya, I embrace you until our meeting, which is near, and give you my mother’s blessing. Love Dunya, your sister, Rodya; love her as she loves you, and know that she loves you boundlessly, more than herself. She is an angel, and you, Rodya, you are everything to us, all our hope and all our trust. If only you are happy, we shall be happy. Do you pray to God, Rodya, as you used to, and do you believe in the goodness of our Creator and Redeemer? I am afraid in my heart that the newest fashionable unbelief may have visited you too. If so, I pray for you. Remember, my dear, how in your childhood, when your father was alive, you used to lisp your prayers on my knees, and how happy we all were then! Goodbye, or, better, until we meet! I embrace you tight, tight, and kiss you countless times.
“Yours till death,
“Pulkheria Raskolnikova.”

Almost the whole time Raskolnikov was reading, from the very beginning of the letter, his face was wet with tears; but when he had finished, it was pale, twisted with a spasm, and a heavy, bilious, malicious smile wound over his lips. He laid his head on his thin, worn pillow and thought, thought for a long time. His heart was beating hard, and his thoughts were in great turmoil. At last he felt stifled and cramped in this yellow little room, like a cupboard or a trunk. His eyes and his mind asked for space. He seized his hat and went out, this time no longer afraid of meeting anyone on the stairs; he had forgotten about it. He set off towards Vasilyevsky Island along V. Prospect, as if hurrying there on business; but, as was his habit, he walked without noticing where he was going, whispering to himself and even talking aloud to himself, which greatly surprised the passers-by. Many took him for a drunk.
## CHAPTER IV

His mother’s letter had tormented him. But about the chief, the capital point, he had not had a moment’s doubt, even while he was still reading the letter. The chief substance of the matter was decided in his head, and decided finally: “This marriage will not happen while I am alive, and to the devil with Mr Luzhin!”

“Because the thing is obvious,” he muttered to himself, grinning and maliciously triumphing in advance at the success of his decision. “No, Mama, no, Dunya, you won’t deceive me!.. And they apologise, too, for not asking my advice and deciding the matter without me! I should think so! They think it can’t be broken off now; well, we shall see whether it can or not! And what a capital excuse: ‘Pyotr Petrovich is such a man of business, such a man of business, that he can’t even get married except by post-chaise, almost by railway.’ No, Dunechka, I see everything, and I know what you mean to talk to me about so much; I know too what you thought about all night, walking about the room, and what you prayed about before the Kazan Mother of God that stands in Mama’s bedroom. It is hard to climb Golgotha. Hm... So it is finally decided: you are pleased to marry a man of business and of reason, Avdotya Romanovna, who has capital of his own (already has capital of his own, that is more solid, more impressive), who holds two posts and shares the convictions of our newest generations (as Mama writes), and who ‘seems kind’, as Dunechka herself remarks. That ‘seems’ is the most magnificent of all! And this same Dunechka is marrying for this same ‘seems’!.. Magnificent! Magnificent!..

“...But I wonder why Mama wrote to me about ‘the newest generations’? Simply to describe the person, or with a further aim: to win me over to Mr Luzhin? Oh, the cunning things! I should like to clear up one more circumstance: how far were they frank with each other, that day and that night, and all the time since? Were all the words between them said straight out, or did both understand that they had the same thing in their hearts and minds, so that there was no point in saying it all aloud and letting things slip for nothing? Probably it was partly like that; one can see from the letter: he seemed abrupt to Mama, a little, and naive Mama went to Dunya with her remarks. And she, of course, was angry and ‘answered with vexation’. I should think so! Who would not be furious, when the thing is clear without naive questions, and when it is decided that there is nothing to say? And why does she write to me: ‘Love Dunya, Rodya, for she loves you more than herself’? Is it not her conscience secretly tormenting her for agreeing to sacrifice her daughter to her son? ‘You are our hope, you are our everything!’ Oh, Mama!..” Anger boiled up in him more and more, and if Mr Luzhin had met him now, he would, it seems, have killed him!

“Hm, it is true,” he went on, following the whirlwind of thoughts that spun in his head, “it is true that one must ‘approach a man gradually and carefully to find out what he is like’; but Mr Luzhin is clear. Above all, ‘a man of business and, it seems, kind’: no small thing, he has taken on the luggage, he is sending the big trunk at his own expense! How can he not be kind? And they, the two of them, the bride and her mother, hire a peasant, in a cart covered with matting (I have travelled like that)! Never mind! Only ninety versts, ‘and from there we shall ride very comfortably third class’, a thousand versts or so. And sensibly: cut your coat according to your cloth; but you, Mr Luzhin, what about you? She is your bride, after all... And you cannot have failed to know that her mother is borrowing on her pension for the journey? Of course, with you it is a joint commercial transaction, an enterprise for mutual advantage and in equal shares, so the expenses are halved too; bread and salt together, but each pays for his own tobacco, as the proverb says. And even here the man of business has cheated them a little: the luggage costs less than their fare, and it may even go for nothing. Do they really not see this, the two of them, or are they not noticing it on purpose? And they are pleased, pleased! And to think that these are only the blossoms, and the real fruits are still to come! For what matters here is not the meanness, not the stinginess, but the tone of it all. For that is the tone of the future after the marriage, a prophecy... And Mama, though, why is she on such a spree? What will she arrive in Petersburg with? With three roubles, or two ‘little notes’, as that... old woman says... hm! What does she hope to live on in Petersburg afterwards? For she has already, for some reason, managed to guess that she cannot live with Dunya after the marriage, even at first? The dear man must have let something slip there somehow, made himself known, though Mama waves it away with both hands: ‘I shall refuse myself.’ What, then, who is she relying on: on her hundred and twenty roubles’ pension, less the deduction for the debt to Afanasy Ivanovich? She knits winter shawls there, and embroiders cuffs, and ruins her old eyes. But the shawls only add twenty roubles a year to the hundred and twenty, that I know. So they are relying after all on the nobility of Mr Luzhin’s feelings: ‘He will offer himself, he will beg us.’ Don’t count on it! And that is how it always is with these beautiful Schillerian souls: to the last moment they dress a man in peacock feathers, to the last moment they hope for good and not for bad; and although they have a presentiment of the other side of the medal, they will on no account say the real word to themselves in advance; the mere thought of it makes them shudder; they wave the truth away with both hands, until the very moment when the dressed-up man makes fools of them with his own hands. I wonder whether Mr Luzhin has any decorations; I bet he has the Anna in his buttonhole, and wears it to dinners with contractors and merchants. Perhaps he will wear it at his wedding too! But to the devil with him!..

“...Well, let Mama be, God be with her, that is how she is; but what about Dunya? Dunechka, my dear, I know you! You were already in your twentieth year when we last saw each other: I understood your character already. Mama writes that ‘Dunechka can bear a great deal’. I knew that. I knew that two and a half years ago, and for two and a half years since I have been thinking about it, about precisely that, that ‘Dunechka can bear a great deal’. If she can bear Mr Svidrigailov, with all the consequences, then she really can bear a great deal. And now they have imagined, she and Mama, that Mr Luzhin too can be borne, setting out his theory of the superiority of wives taken from destitution and made beholden to their husbands, and setting it out almost at the first meeting. Well, suppose he ‘let it slip’, though he is a man of reason (so that perhaps he did not let it slip at all, but meant precisely to make it clear as soon as possible); but Dunya, Dunya? The man is clear to her, and she has to live with the man. She would eat nothing but black bread and drink water with it, but she would not sell her soul, she would not give up her moral freedom for comfort; she would not give it up for the whole of Schleswig-Holstein, let alone for Mr Luzhin. No, Dunya was not like that, as far as I knew her, and... well, of course, she has not changed now either!.. What is there to say! The Svidrigailovs are hard to bear! It is hard to drag around the provinces all one’s life as a governess for two hundred roubles; but still I know that my sister would sooner become a negro slave to a planter, or a Latvian serf to a Baltic German, than debase her spirit and her moral sense by binding herself to a man she does not respect and with whom she has nothing to do, for ever, for her own personal advantage alone! And even if Mr Luzhin were made all of the purest gold or of one whole diamond, even then she would not agree to become Mr Luzhin’s lawful concubine! Why does she agree now, then? What is the trick? What is the answer to the riddle? The thing is clear: for herself, for her own comfort, even to save herself from death, she would not sell herself; but for someone else, there, she does sell herself! For someone dear, for someone adored, she will sell herself! That is what our whole trick consists of: for her brother, for her mother she will sell herself! She will sell everything! Oh, in this case we will even crush our moral sense if need be; freedom, peace, even conscience, everything, everything we will take to the flea market. Let life go! As long as these beloved beings of ours are happy. More than that, we will invent our own casuistry, we will learn from the Jesuits, and for a while, perhaps, we will even calm ourselves, convince ourselves that it is necessary, really necessary for a good end. That is just how we are, and everything is as clear as day. It is clear that it is none other than Rodion Romanovich Raskolnikov who is the point here and stands in the foreground. Well, of course: she can arrange his happiness, keep him at the university, make him a partner in the office, secure his whole fate; perhaps he will be a rich man later on, honoured, respected, and perhaps even end his life a famous man! And Mother? But this is Rodya, precious Rodya, the first-born! How could one not sacrifice even such a daughter for such a first-born! Oh, loving and unjust hearts! Why, here we would not even refuse Sonechka’s lot, perhaps! Sonechka, Sonechka Marmeladova, eternal Sonechka, as long as the world stands! Have you both fully measured the sacrifice, the sacrifice? Have you? Is it within your strength? Is it for the good? Is it reasonable? Do you know, Dunechka, that Sonechka’s lot is no fouler than the lot with Mr Luzhin? ‘There can be no love here,’ Mama writes. And what if, besides love, there can be no respect either, but on the contrary there is already aversion, contempt, disgust, what then? Then it turns out that once again one will have to ‘keep oneself clean’. Is that not so? Do you understand, do you understand what that cleanliness means? Do you understand that Luzhin’s cleanliness is just the same as Sonechka’s cleanliness, and perhaps even worse, fouler, viler, because with you, Dunechka, after all, there is a calculation on some extra comfort, while there it is simply a matter of starving to death! ‘It costs dear, dear, Dunechka, that cleanliness!’ Well, and if it becomes too much for you afterwards, will you repent? How much sorrow, grief, cursing, how many tears hidden from everyone, for you are no Marfa Petrovna, are you? And what will happen to Mother then? For she is uneasy even now, she is tormented; and then, when she sees everything clearly? And to me?.. Yes, what have you really been thinking of me? I do not want your sacrifice, Dunechka, I do not want it, Mama! It will not be, while I am alive, it will not be, it will not be! I do not accept it!”
He suddenly came to himself and stopped.

“It will not be? And what will you do to stop it? Forbid it? And what right have you? What can you promise them in return, to have such a right? To devote your whole fate, your whole future to them, when you have finished your course and got a post? We have heard that, but that is pie in the sky; and now? For something has to be done now, do you understand that? And what are you doing now? Robbing them. For the money comes to them as a loan on a hundred-rouble pension and as an advance from the Svidrigailov gentry! How will you protect them from the Svidrigailovs, from Afanasy Ivanovich Vakhrushin, you future millionaire, you Zeus who disposes of their fate? In ten years’ time? In ten years Mother will have had time to go blind from shawls, and perhaps from tears too; she will waste away from fasting; and your sister? Well, think, what may become of your sister in ten years, or during those ten years? Have you guessed?”

So he tormented and teased himself with these questions, even with a kind of pleasure. But all these questions were not new, not sudden, but old, aching, long-standing. They had begun to torture him long ago and had worn out his heart. Long, long ago all this present anguish had been born in him; it had grown, accumulated, and lately it had ripened and concentrated, taking the form of a terrible, wild and fantastic question, which had tormented his heart and mind, irresistibly demanding to be resolved. Now his mother’s letter had suddenly struck him like a thunderbolt. It was clear that now he must not pine, not suffer passively, with mere reasoning that the questions could not be resolved, but must certainly do something, and at once, and quickly. At all costs he must make up his mind, to something at least, or...
“Or give up life altogether!” he suddenly cried in a frenzy. “Accept fate obediently as it is, once and for all, and stifle everything in myself, renouncing every right to act, to live and to love!”

“Do you understand, do you understand, my dear sir, what it means when there is nowhere else to go?” Marmeladov’s question of yesterday suddenly came back to him. “For every man must have somewhere he can go...”

Suddenly he started: a thought, also from yesterday, had flashed through his head again. But he did not start because this thought had flashed through it. For he had known, he had sensed, that it would certainly “flash through”, and he had already been waiting for it; and this thought was not from yesterday at all. But the difference was that a month ago, and even yesterday, it had only been a dream, while now... now it appeared suddenly not as a dream, but in some new, menacing and quite unfamiliar form, and he suddenly realised this himself... The blood beat in his head, and his eyes went dark.

He looked round hastily; he was looking for something. He wanted to sit down, and he was looking for a bench; he was walking along K. Boulevard at that moment. There was a bench ahead, about a hundred paces away. He walked as fast as he could; but on the way a little adventure happened to him, which for a few minutes drew all his attention.

Looking out for the bench, he noticed a woman walking about twenty paces ahead of him, but at first he paid no attention to her, any more than to all the other objects that had flickered before him until then. It had already happened to him many times, for instance, to walk home and not remember at all the way he had come, and he was used to walking like that by now. But there was something so strange about the woman walking ahead, something that caught the eye from the very first glance, that little by little his attention began to fasten on her, at first reluctantly and as if with annoyance, and then more and more firmly. He suddenly wanted to understand what exactly was so strange about this woman. In the first place, she must be a very young girl, and she was walking in such heat bareheaded, without a parasol or gloves, swinging her arms in a funny way. She had on a little dress of light silk material, but it too was put on very oddly, hardly fastened, and torn at the back at the waist, at the very top of the skirt; a whole piece hung loose and dangled. A little scarf was thrown over her bare neck, but it stuck out somehow crookedly and to one side. To crown it all, the girl was walking unsteadily, stumbling and even swaying from side to side. This meeting finally roused all Raskolnikov’s attention. He came up with the girl right by the bench; but when she reached the bench she simply collapsed on it, in the corner, threw her head back on the back of the bench and closed her eyes, apparently from extreme exhaustion. Looking closely at her, he guessed at once that she was completely drunk. It was strange and wild to look at such a sight. He even wondered whether he was mistaken. Before him was an extremely young little face, sixteen or so, perhaps even only fifteen: small, fair-haired, pretty, but all flushed and as if swollen. The girl seemed to understand very little by now; she had crossed one leg over the other, showing much more of it than was proper, and by every sign she was very little aware that she was in the street.

Raskolnikov did not sit down, and did not want to go away, but stood before her in bewilderment. This boulevard is always deserted, and now, at past one o’clock and in such heat, there was almost no one. And yet a little way off, about fifteen paces, at the edge of the boulevard, a gentleman had stopped who, by every sign, would very much have liked to go up to the girl too, with some purposes of his own. He too had probably seen her from a distance and had been catching up with her, but Raskolnikov had got in his way. He kept throwing angry looks at him, trying, though, not to let him notice them, and waited impatiently for his turn, for the annoying ragamuffin to go away. The thing was clear. The gentleman was about thirty, stout, fat, ruddy as blood and milk, with pink lips and a little moustache, and very foppishly dressed. Raskolnikov was terribly angry; he suddenly wanted somehow to insult this fat dandy. He left the girl for a minute and went up to the gentleman.
“Hey, you, Svidrigailov! What do you want here?” he shouted, clenching his fists and laughing with lips that were foaming with rage.
“What does this mean?” the gentleman asked sternly, frowning and haughtily surprised.
“Clear off, that’s what!”
“How dare you, you scoundrel!..”

And he raised his riding whip. Raskolnikov rushed at him with his fists, not even reckoning that the stout gentleman could deal with two of his kind. But at that moment someone seized him firmly from behind; a policeman had come between them.
“That will do, gentlemen; no fighting in public places, if you please. What do you want? Who are you?” he turned sternly to Raskolnikov, taking in his rags.
Raskolnikov looked at him attentively. It was a fine soldierly face with grey moustaches and side-whiskers and a sensible look.

“You are just the man I need,” he cried, seizing him by the arm. “I am a former student, Raskolnikov... You can find that out too,” he turned to the gentleman, “but you, come along, I will show you something...”
And, seizing the policeman by the arm, he dragged him to the bench.

“Here, look, she is completely drunk; she was walking along the boulevard just now; who knows what sort she is, but she does not look as if she does it for a living. Most likely someone gave her drink somewhere and took advantage of her... for the first time... do you understand? and then let her out into the street like that. Look how her dress is torn, look how it is put on: someone dressed her, she did not dress herself, and they were clumsy hands that dressed her, a man’s hands. That is plain. And now look over here: this dandy I was about to fight with just now is a stranger to me, I see him for the first time; but he too marked her down on the way just now, drunk, not knowing what she is doing, and now he terribly wants to come up and get hold of her, since she is in such a state, and take her off somewhere... And that is surely so; believe me, I am not mistaken. I saw him myself watching her and following her, only I got in his way, and now he is waiting for me to go. There, he has moved off a little now, he is standing as if rolling a cigarette... How can we stop him? How can we send her home? Think!”

The policeman understood and grasped everything in a moment. The fat gentleman, of course, was clear; that left the girl. The policeman bent over her to look more closely, and sincere compassion showed in his features.

“Ah, what a pity!” he said, shaking his head. “Quite a child still. Somebody took advantage, that’s just it. Listen, miss,” he began calling to her, “where do you live?” The girl opened her tired, bleary eyes, looked dully at the men questioning her, and waved them away.

“Listen,” said Raskolnikov, “here” (he fumbled in his pocket and pulled out twenty kopecks; he found them), “here, take a cab and tell him to drive her to her address. If only we could find out the address!”
“Miss, eh, miss?” the policeman began again, taking the money. “I’ll get you a cab right now and take you myself. Where shall I take you? Eh? Where do you live?”
“Go 'way!.. Pestering me!..” the girl muttered, and waved them away again.

“Ah, ah, how bad! Ah, how shameful, miss, what a shame!” He shook his head again, shaming her, pitying her and indignant. “That’s a problem!” he turned to Raskolnikov, and at the same time, in passing, looked him up and down again. He must have seemed strange to him too: in such rags, and yet handing out money!
“Did you find her far from here?” he asked him.
“I tell you: she was walking ahead of me, staggering, right here on the boulevard. As soon as she got to the bench, she collapsed.”

“Ah, what shamefulness there is in the world nowadays, Lord! Such a simple little thing, and already drunk! Somebody took advantage, that’s how it is! And her little dress is torn too... Ah, what depravity there is nowadays!.. And she may well be of good family, from some poor ones... There are many like that nowadays. To look at her, one of the delicate ones, just like a young lady,” and he bent over her again.
Perhaps he too had daughters growing up like that, “just like young ladies and delicate ones”, with the manners of the well brought up and with every fashionable affectation already picked up...
“The main thing,” Raskolnikov fussed, “is how to stop this scoundrel! He will only abuse her! One can see by heart what he wants; look at the scoundrel, he won’t go away!”

Raskolnikov spoke loudly and pointed straight at him. The man heard and was about to get angry again, but thought better of it and confined himself to a contemptuous look. Then he slowly moved off another ten paces or so and stopped again.
“We can stop them, sir,” the sergeant answered thoughtfully. “If only she would say where to take her; but as it is... Miss, eh, miss!” He bent down again.
She suddenly opened her eyes wide, looked attentively, as if she had understood something, got up from the bench and walked back in the direction she had come from.

“Pah, shameless things, pestering me!” she said, waving them away once more. She walked fast, but still staggering badly. The dandy followed her, but along another path, without taking his eyes off her.
“Don’t worry, I won’t let him, sir,” the moustached man said firmly, and set off after them.
“Eh, what depravity there is nowadays!” he repeated aloud, sighing.
At that moment something seemed to sting Raskolnikov; in an instant he seemed to be turned upside down.
“Listen, hey!” he shouted after the moustached man.
The man turned round.
“Let them be! What is it to you? Drop it! Let him have his fun” (he pointed at the dandy). “What is it to you?”
The policeman did not understand and stared at him wide-eyed. Raskolnikov laughed.
“Eh-eh!” said the policeman, waving his hand, and went off after the dandy and the girl, probably taking Raskolnikov either for a madman or for something even worse.

“He has carried off my twenty kopecks,” Raskolnikov said angrily, left alone. “Well, let him take something from the other one too and let the girl go with him, and that will be the end of it... And why did I get mixed up in helping here! Is it for me to help? Have I the right to help? Let them swallow one another alive: what is it to me? And how did I dare give away those twenty kopecks? Are they mine?”

In spite of these strange words, he felt very heavy at heart. He sat down on the bench, now empty. His thoughts were scattered... And in general it was hard for him at that moment to think about anything at all. He would have liked to forget himself completely, forget everything, then wake up and begin all over again...

“Poor girl!..” he said, looking at the empty corner of the bench. “She will come to, she will cry, then her mother will find out... First she will beat her, and then she will thrash her, painfully and shamefully, and perhaps drive her out... And if she does not drive her out, the Darya Frantsevnas will sniff her out all the same, and my girl will start slipping out here and there... Then straight away the hospital (that is always how it is with those who live with very honest mothers and get up to mischief on the quiet), and then... and then the hospital again... drink... taverns... and the hospital again... in two or three years, a wreck, so her whole life will have been nineteen years or eighteen in all... Haven’t I seen such girls? And how did they become like that? Why, just like this... Pah! But let it be! That, they say, is how it ought to be. A certain percentage, they say, must go every year... somewhere... to the devil, it must be, so as to freshen up the rest and not get in their way. A percentage! Splendid little words they have, really: so soothing, so scientific. Once you say ‘percentage’, there is nothing to worry about. Now if it were another word, well then... it might be more disturbing... And what if Dunechka somehow falls into the percentage!.. If not that one, then another?..

“But where am I going?” he suddenly thought. “Strange. I set out for some reason. As soon as I read the letter, I set out... To Vasilyevsky Island, to Razumikhin, that is where I was going, now... I remember. But why, though? And how did the idea of going to Razumikhin come into my head just now? That is remarkable.”

He wondered at himself. Razumikhin was one of his former fellow students at the university. It is remarkable that Raskolnikov, while he was at the university, had almost no friends; he kept away from everyone, visited no one, and did not like receiving anyone himself. And soon everyone turned away from him too. He somehow took no part in common gatherings, or in conversations, or in amusements, or in anything. He studied hard, without sparing himself, and for that he was respected, but no one liked him. He was very poor, and somehow haughtily proud and uncommunicative, as if he were keeping something to himself. To some of his fellow students it seemed that he looked down on them all as on children, as if he were ahead of them all in development, and knowledge, and convictions, and as if he regarded their convictions and interests as something inferior.

But with Razumikhin he had for some reason got on, that is, not exactly got on, but he was more communicative, more open with him. Indeed, with Razumikhin it was impossible to be on any other terms. He was an unusually cheerful and sociable fellow, kind to the point of simplicity. But under this simplicity there were also depth and dignity. The best of his fellow students understood this, and everyone loved him. He was far from stupid, though sometimes he really was a bit simple. His appearance was striking: tall, thin, always badly shaved, black-haired. Sometimes he made a row and had the reputation of a strong man. Once at night, in company, he knocked down with one blow a guardian of the peace who was a good six foot four. He could drink without end, but he could also not drink at all; sometimes he played pranks that went too far, but he could also do without pranks entirely. Razumikhin was remarkable too in that no failures ever discouraged him, and no bad circumstances, it seemed, could crush him. He could lodge even on a roof, and put up with hellish hunger and extraordinary cold. He was very poor, and kept himself entirely on his own, earning money by odd jobs of one kind or another. He knew a bottomless number of sources from which he could draw, by work, of course. Once he went a whole winter without heating his room at all, and maintained that it was even more pleasant, because one sleeps better in the cold. At present he too had been obliged to leave the university, but not for long, and he was hurrying with all his strength to put his affairs right so that he could continue. Raskolnikov had not been to see him for about four months, and Razumikhin did not even know where he lived. Once, about two months ago, they had met in the street, but Raskolnikov had turned away and even crossed to the other side, so that he would not be noticed. And Razumikhin, though he did notice, walked past, not wishing to trouble his friend.
## CHAPTER V

“It is true, I was meaning not long ago to ask Razumikhin for work, to get me lessons or something...” Raskolnikov thought it through, “but how can he help me now? Suppose he gets me lessons, suppose he even shares his last kopeck with me, if he has a kopeck, so that I could even buy boots and mend my clothes to go to lessons... hm... Well, and then? What shall I do with five-kopeck pieces? Is that what I need now? Really, it is ridiculous that I set out for Razumikhin’s...”

The question of why he had set out for Razumikhin’s now troubled him more than even he himself realised; uneasily he kept searching for some sinister meaning for himself in what seemed the most ordinary action.
“What, did I really want to put the whole thing right with Razumikhin alone, and find the way out of everything in Razumikhin?” he asked himself in surprise.
He thought and rubbed his forehead, and, strange to say, somehow by chance, suddenly and almost of itself, after very long reflection, a very strange thought came into his head.

“Hm... to Razumikhin,” he said suddenly, quite calmly, as if it were a final decision, “to Razumikhin I shall go, of course... but not now... I shall go to him... the day after, after that, when that is already over and everything begins anew...”
And suddenly he came to himself.
“After that,” he cried, jumping up from the bench, “but is that going to happen? Is it really going to happen?”

He left the bench and walked off, almost ran; he was about to turn back towards home, but suddenly he felt a terrible loathing for going home: there, in that corner, in that terrible cupboard, all this had been ripening for more than a month now; and he walked on wherever his feet took him.

His nervous trembling had turned into something like a fever; he even felt a chill; in such heat he was growing cold. As if with an effort, almost unconsciously, from some inner necessity, he began to stare at every object he came across, as if searching hard for distraction; but he did not succeed very well, and kept falling into thought. And when, with a start, he raised his head again and looked around, he immediately forgot what he had just been thinking about and even where he was going. In this way he walked the whole length of Vasilyevsky Island, came out at the Little Neva, crossed the bridge and turned towards the Islands. The greenery and freshness pleased his tired eyes at first, used as they were to the dust of the city, to lime and to huge houses that crowded and oppressed him. Here there was no stuffiness, no stench, no taverns. But soon these new, pleasant sensations too turned sick and irritating. Sometimes he stopped before some summer villa decked in greenery, looked through the fence, and saw in the distance, on balconies and terraces, women in fine dresses and children running in the garden. The flowers especially caught his attention; he looked at them longest of all. He also met splendid carriages, men and women on horseback; he followed them with his eyes curiously and forgot them before they had disappeared from sight. Once he stopped and counted his money: it turned out to be about thirty kopecks. “Twenty to the policeman, three to Nastasya for the letter, so I gave the Marmeladovs forty-seven or fifty kopecks yesterday,” he thought, reckoning for some reason; but soon he even forgot why he had taken the money out of his pocket. He remembered it as he passed an eating house, a sort of cheap tavern, and felt that he was hungry. Going into the eating house, he drank a glass of vodka and ate a pie with some sort of filling. He finished it on the road again. He had not drunk vodka for a very long time, and it took effect at once, though he had drunk only one glass. His legs suddenly grew heavy, and he began to feel a strong urge to sleep. He set off home; but when he had got as far as Petrovsky Island, he stopped in complete exhaustion, left the road, went into the bushes, fell on the grass and at that very moment fell asleep.

In a sick state, dreams are often distinguished by an extraordinary vividness and brightness and an extreme likeness to reality. Sometimes a monstrous picture takes shape, but the setting and the whole course of the scene are at the same time so probable, and with such fine, unexpected details, which yet fit artistically into the fullness of the picture, that the dreamer himself could not invent them awake, even if he were as great an artist as Pushkin or Turgenev. Such dreams, sick dreams, are always remembered for a long time and make a strong impression on a man’s disordered and already overexcited organism.

Raskolnikov had a terrible dream. He dreamed of his childhood, back in their little town. He is about seven and is walking with his father outside the town on a holiday, towards evening. The day is grey and stifling, the place is exactly as it had survived in his memory; indeed in his memory it had faded much more than it appeared now in the dream. The little town lies open as if on the palm of a hand, not a willow anywhere around; somewhere very far away, at the very edge of the sky, a little wood shows black. A few paces from the last market garden of the town stands a tavern, a big tavern, which always made a most unpleasant impression on him, and even frightened him, when he walked past it with his father. There was always such a crowd there, they shouted, guffawed, swore, sang so hideously and hoarsely, and fought so often; such drunken and fearful faces always hung about the tavern... When he met them, he pressed close to his father and trembled all over. By the tavern runs the road, a country track, always dusty, and the dust on it is always so black. It winds on further, and about three hundred paces on it curves to the right round the town cemetery. In the middle of the cemetery is a stone church with a green dome, to which he went with his father and mother two or three times a year to Mass, when requiems were sung for his grandmother, who had died long before and whom he had never seen. They always took with them on these occasions funeral rice on a white dish, wrapped in a napkin, and the rice was sweet, made of rice and raisins pressed into the rice in the shape of a cross. He loved this church and its old icons, mostly without frames, and the old priest with his trembling head. Beside his grandmother’s grave, which had a stone slab on it, was the little grave of his younger brother, who had died at six months old and whom he had not known at all either and could not remember; but he had been told that he had a little brother, and every time he visited the cemetery he crossed himself religiously and reverently over the little grave, bowed to it and kissed it. And now he dreams: he and his father are walking along the road to the cemetery and passing the tavern; he is holding his father’s hand and looking round fearfully at the tavern. A particular circumstance catches his attention: this time there seems to be some festivity here, a crowd of townswomen in their best clothes, peasant women, their husbands and all sorts of riffraff. They are all drunk, they are all singing songs, and by the tavern steps stands a cart, but a strange cart. It is one of those big carts to which big dray-horses are harnessed and in which goods and barrels of wine are carried. He always loved to watch those huge dray-horses, with their long manes and thick legs, walking calmly with measured steps and pulling a whole mountain behind them without the least strain, as if it were even easier for them with loads than without. But now, strange to say, a small, thin, sorrel peasant nag was harnessed to such a big cart, one of those which, as he had often seen, strain themselves sometimes with some high load of wood or hay, especially when the load sticks in the mud or in a rut, and the peasants always beat them so painfully, so painfully with their whips, sometimes even right on the muzzle and on the eyes, and he is so sorry, so sorry to see it that he almost cries, and Mama always used to lead him away from the window. But now suddenly it grows very noisy: out of the tavern, with shouts and songs and balalaikas, come some huge peasants, dead drunk, in red and blue shirts, with their coats thrown over their shoulders. “Get in, everybody get in!” shouts one of them, still young, with a thick neck and a fleshy face as red as a carrot. “I’ll drive you all, get in!” But at once there is laughter and exclamations:
“A nag like that pull it!”
“Have you gone out of your mind, Mikolka? Harnessing a little mare like that to a cart like that!”
“Why, the sorrel must be twenty years old, lads!”

“Get in, I’ll drive you all!” Mikolka shouts again, jumping first into the cart; he takes the reins and stands up at full height in the front. “The bay went off with Matvey just now,” he shouts from the cart, “and this little mare, lads, only breaks my heart: I could kill her, it seems, she eats her bread for nothing. I say get in! I’ll make her gallop! She’ll gallop!” And he takes the whip in his hands, getting ready with relish to flog the sorrel.
“Get in, then, why not!” they guffaw in the crowd. “Do you hear, she’ll gallop!”
“She hasn’t galloped for ten years, I bet.”
“She’ll gallop!”
“Don’t spare her, lads, everybody take a whip, get ready!”
“That’s it! Flog her!”

They all climb into Mikolka’s cart with guffaws and jokes. Six or so have climbed in, and there is room for more. They take one woman with them, fat and rosy. She is in red calico, with a beaded headdress, with felt boots on her feet; she cracks nuts and laughs. Around them in the crowd they are laughing too, and indeed, how could they not laugh: a wretched little mare like that is going to pull such a load at a gallop! Two lads in the cart take a whip each at once, to help Mikolka. There is a cry of “Gee up!”, the little nag pulls with all her strength, but far from galloping, she can hardly even manage a walk; she only shuffles her feet, grunts, and cringes under the blows of the three whips, which rain down on her like peas. The laughter in the cart and in the crowd doubles, but Mikolka is angry and in a rage flogs the little mare with quicker and quicker blows, as if he really thinks she will gallop.
“Let me in too, lads!” shouts one lad in the crowd who has got a taste for it.
“Get in! Everybody get in!” shouts Mikolka. “She’ll pull you all. I’ll flog her to death!” And he lashes and lashes, and in his frenzy no longer knows what to beat her with.
“Papa, Papa,” he cries to his father, “Papa, what are they doing? Papa, they are beating the poor horse!”

“Come along, come along!” says his father. “They are drunk, they are fooling about, the fools: come along, don’t look!” And he tries to lead him away, but he tears himself out of his hands and, beside himself, runs to the horse. But the poor horse is in a bad way already. She is gasping, she stops, pulls again, almost falls.
“Flog her to death!” shouts Mikolka. “That’s what it’s come to. I’ll flog her to death!”
“Have you no cross on you, you devil?” shouts an old man from the crowd.
“Whoever saw a little horse like that pull a load like that?” adds another.
“You’ll kill her!” shouts a third.
“Don’t touch! She’s my property! I do what I like. Get in, more of you! Everybody get in! I want her to gallop, no matter what!..”

Suddenly a volley of laughter breaks out and drowns everything: the little mare could not bear the quickening blows and in her helplessness began to kick. Even the old man could not help grinning. And indeed: such a wretched little mare, and she kicks too!
Two lads from the crowd get hold of a whip each as well and run to the horse to flog her from the sides. Each runs to his own side.
“On the muzzle, lash her on the eyes, on the eyes!” shouts Mikolka.

“A song, lads!” shouts someone from the cart, and everyone in the cart joins in. A rollicking song rings out, a tambourine jingles, there is whistling in the refrains. The woman cracks nuts and laughs.

...He runs beside the horse, he runs in front, he sees them lashing her on the eyes, right on the eyes! He is crying. His heart rises in him, tears flow. One of those flogging catches him across the face; he does not feel it, he wrings his hands, he cries out, he rushes to a grey-haired old man with a grey beard, who is shaking his head and condemning it all. A woman takes him by the hand and tries to lead him away; but he tears himself free and runs to the horse again. She is at her last efforts, but she begins to kick once more.

“The devil take you!” Mikolka cries in a fury. He throws down the whip, bends down and pulls out from the bottom of the cart a long, thick shaft, takes it by the end in both hands and swings it with an effort over the sorrel.
“He’ll smash her!” they shout all around.
“He’ll kill her!”
“She’s my property!” shouts Mikolka, and brings the shaft down with all his might. There is a heavy thud.
“Flog her, flog her! Why have you stopped?” shout voices from the crowd.

And Mikolka swings a second time, and a second blow falls with all his might on the back of the unhappy nag. She sinks down on her haunches, but leaps up and pulls, pulls with all her last strength in different directions, trying to move the cart; but on all sides they meet her with six whips, and the shaft rises again and falls a third time, then a fourth, steadily, with a full swing. Mikolka is furious that he cannot kill her with one blow.
“She’s tough!” they shout all around.
“She’ll fall in a minute, lads, sure enough, and that’ll be the end of her!” shouts an enthusiast from the crowd.
“Take an axe to her, why not! Finish her off at once,” shouts a third.

“Eh, may the mosquitoes eat you! Make way!” Mikolka screams in a frenzy; he throws down the shaft, bends into the cart again and pulls out an iron crowbar. “Look out!” he shouts, and with all his might he deals his poor little horse a stunning blow with a full swing. The blow crashes down; the little mare staggers, sinks down, tries to pull, but the crowbar comes down on her back again with a full swing, and she falls to the ground as if all four legs had been cut from under her at once.

“Finish her off!” shouts Mikolka, and leaps down from the cart as if beside himself. Several lads, also red and drunk, seize whatever comes to hand, whips, sticks, the shaft, and run to the dying mare. Mikolka stands at her side and begins to beat her at random on the back with the crowbar. The nag stretches out her muzzle, sighs heavily, and dies.
“He’s done for her!” they shout in the crowd.
“Why wouldn’t she gallop!”
“She’s my property!” shouts Mikolka, with the crowbar in his hands and his eyes bloodshot. He stands there as if sorry that there is no one left to beat.
“Well, there really is no cross on you, it seems!” many voices now shout from the crowd.

But the poor boy is beside himself. With a cry he forces his way through the crowd to the sorrel, puts his arms around her dead, bleeding muzzle and kisses it, kisses her on the eyes, on the lips... Then suddenly he jumps up and in a frenzy throws himself with his little fists on Mikolka. At that moment his father, who has long been chasing after him, at last seizes him and carries him out of the crowd.
“Come along! Come along!” he says to him. “Let us go home!”
“Papa! Why did they... kill... the poor horse!” he sobs, but his breath catches, and the words burst out in cries from his tight chest.

“They are drunk, they are fooling about, it’s not our business, come along!” says his father. He puts his arms around his father, but his chest is tight, tight. He tries to get his breath, to cry out, and wakes up.
He woke up all in a sweat, his hair wet with sweat, gasping, and raised himself in horror.
“Thank God, it was only a dream!” he said, sitting up under a tree and drawing deep breaths. “But what is this? Is a fever beginning in me: such a hideous dream!”
His whole body felt as if it had been beaten; his soul was troubled and dark. He put his elbows on his knees and propped his head in both hands.

“God!” he exclaimed. “Can it be, can it be that I shall really take an axe, that I shall strike her on the head, smash her skull... that I shall slip in the sticky, warm blood, break open the lock, steal and tremble; hide, all covered in blood... with the axe... Lord, can it be?”
He was trembling like a leaf as he said this.

“But what am I doing!” he went on, raising himself again, as if in deep amazement. “I knew, after all, that I could not bear it, so why have I been tormenting myself until now? Why, only yesterday, yesterday, when I went to make that... rehearsal, I understood perfectly yesterday that I could not stand it... What am I doing now, then? Why have I still been doubting until now? Why, yesterday, coming down the stairs, I said myself that it was base, loathsome, low, low... why, the mere thought of it made me sick in waking life and threw me into horror...

“No, I cannot stand it, I cannot stand it! Let it be, let there even be no doubt at all about all those calculations, let everything that has been decided this month be as clear as day, as just as arithmetic. Lord! I still shall not dare to do it! I cannot stand it, I cannot stand it!.. Why, then, why until now...”

He got to his feet, looked round in surprise, as if wondering even that he had come here, and went towards T. Bridge. He was pale, his eyes were burning, there was exhaustion in all his limbs, but suddenly he seemed to breathe more easily. He felt that he had already thrown off that terrible burden that had weighed on him so long, and suddenly his soul felt light and at peace. “Lord!” he prayed, “show me my way, and I renounce this accursed... dream of mine!”

As he crossed the bridge, he looked quietly and calmly at the Neva, at the bright sunset of the bright red sun. In spite of his weakness he did not even feel tired. It was as if an abscess in his heart, which had been festering all month, had suddenly burst. Freedom, freedom! He was free now from those spells, from sorcery, from enchantment, from obsession!

Later, when he remembered this time and everything that happened to him in those days, minute by minute, point by point, feature by feature, he was always struck almost superstitiously by one circumstance, which in essence was not very extraordinary, but which always seemed to him afterwards to be a kind of predetermination of his fate.

Namely: he could never understand or explain to himself why, tired and worn out as he was, when it would have been best of all for him to go home by the shortest and most direct way, he went home by way of the Haymarket, where he had no need at all to go. The detour was not great, but it was obvious and completely unnecessary. Of course, dozens of times it had happened to him to come home without remembering the streets he had walked through. But why, he always asked, why did such an important meeting, so decisive for him, and at the same time so utterly accidental, in the Haymarket (where he had no reason even to go), come just now, at such an hour, at such a minute in his life, precisely when his mind was in such a mood and in precisely such circumstances, the only ones in which this meeting could have the most decisive and most final effect on his whole fate? As if it had been lying in wait for him there on purpose!

It was about nine o’clock when he crossed the Haymarket. All the traders at their tables, on their trays, in their shops and stalls, were shutting up their establishments, or taking down and putting away their wares, and going home, as were their customers. Round the cook-shops on the ground floors, in the dirty, stinking courtyards of the Haymarket houses, and most of all by the taverns, crowds of all sorts of tradesmen and ragged people were gathered. Raskolnikov liked these places especially, as well as all the alleys nearby, when he went out into the street with no aim. Here his rags attracted no one’s haughty attention, and one could walk about looking however one liked without scandalising anyone. Right by K. Lane, on the corner, a tradesman and a woman, his wife, were selling goods from two tables: thread, tape, cotton kerchiefs and so on. They too were getting up to go home, but they had lingered, talking to an acquaintance who had come up. This acquaintance was Lizaveta Ivanovna, or simply Lizaveta, as everyone called her, the younger sister of that same old woman, Alyona Ivanovna, a collegiate registrar’s widow and moneylender, whom Raskolnikov had visited the day before when he came to pawn his watch and make his rehearsal... He had long known all about this Lizaveta, and she even knew him a little. She was a tall, clumsy, timid and humble woman, almost simple-minded, thirty-five years old, who was in complete slavery to her sister, worked for her day and night, trembled before her and even suffered beatings from her. She stood there thinking, with a bundle, in front of the tradesman and his wife, and listened to them attentively. They were explaining something to her with special warmth. When Raskolnikov suddenly saw her, a strange sensation, like the deepest astonishment, seized him, although there was nothing astonishing in this meeting.
“You should settle it yourself, Lizaveta Ivanovna,” the tradesman was saying loudly. “Come round tomorrow, about seven o’clock. They’ll be there too.”
“Tomorrow?” Lizaveta said slowly and thoughtfully, as if unable to decide.

“My, how Alyona Ivanovna has frightened you!” the trader’s wife rattled on; she was a lively little woman. “I look at you, and you’re just like a little child. And she isn’t even your own sister, only a half-sister, and see what a hold she has taken over you.”

“And don’t say anything to Alyona Ivanovna this time,” the husband interrupted. “That’s my advice. Just come round to us without asking. It’s a profitable business. Your sister can think it over herself afterwards.”
“Shall I come, then?”
“About seven, tomorrow; and someone from them will be there; you can settle it yourself.”
“And we’ll put the samovar on,” added the wife.
“All right, I’ll come,” said Lizaveta, still thinking it over, and slowly began to move off.

Raskolnikov had already passed by and heard no more. He passed quietly, unnoticed, trying not to miss a single word. His first astonishment gave way little by little to horror, as if a frost had passed down his spine. He had learned, he had suddenly, abruptly and quite unexpectedly learned, that tomorrow, at exactly seven o’clock in the evening, Lizaveta, the old woman’s sister and the only person who lived with her, would not be at home, and that, therefore, the old woman, at exactly seven o’clock in the evening, would be at home alone.

There were only a few steps left to his lodging. He went in like a man condemned to death. He did not reason about anything and was completely unable to reason; but with his whole being he suddenly felt that he no longer had any freedom of reason or will, and that everything had suddenly been decided finally.

Of course, even if he had had to wait whole years for a convenient chance, even then, having the plan, he could not have counted for certain on a more obvious step towards the success of that plan than the one that had suddenly presented itself just now. In any case, it would have been hard to find out the day before, and for certain, with greater precision and with the least risk, without any dangerous questions and inquiries, that tomorrow, at such an hour, such and such an old woman, on whom an attempt was being prepared, would be at home quite alone.
## CHAPTER VI

Later on Raskolnikov happened to find out why the tradesman and his wife had invited Lizaveta to their place. It was the most ordinary business and there was nothing special about it. A family that had come to town and fallen on hard times was selling things, clothes and so on, all women’s things. Since it was not profitable to sell at the market, they were looking for a dealer, and Lizaveta did that kind of work: she took commissions, went about on business and had a large practice, because she was very honest and always named the lowest price: whatever price she named, that was how it was. In general she spoke little, and, as has already been said, she was so humble and timid...

But Raskolnikov had lately become superstitious. Traces of the superstition remained in him for a long time afterwards, almost indelibly. And in this whole affair he was always inclined afterwards to see something strange, as it were, mysterious, as if particular influences and coincidences were present. As far back as the winter, a student he knew, Pokorev, when leaving for Kharkov, had happened to mention to him in conversation the address of the old woman Alyona Ivanovna, in case he should ever need to pawn anything. For a long time he did not go to her, because he had lessons and was managing somehow. About six weeks ago he remembered the address; he had two things fit for pawning: his father’s old silver watch and a little gold ring with three little red stones of some kind, given him by his sister as a keepsake when they parted. He decided to take the ring; having found the old woman, at the very first glance, before he knew anything special about her, he felt an irresistible loathing for her; he took two “little notes” from her and on the way went into a wretched little tavern. He asked for tea, sat down and fell into deep thought. A strange thought was pecking its way out in his head, like a chick out of an egg, and it very, very much absorbed him.

Almost beside him, at another little table, sat a student whom he did not know at all and did not remember, and a young officer. They had played billiards and begun to drink tea. Suddenly he heard the student telling the officer about the moneylender, Alyona Ivanovna, a collegiate secretary’s widow, and giving him her address. This alone seemed somehow strange to Raskolnikov: he had just come from there, and here they were talking about her. Of course it was chance; but he could not shake off one most unusual impression, and here someone seemed to be doing him a service: the student suddenly began telling his companion various details about this Alyona Ivanovna.

“She’s a fine one,” he was saying. “You can always get money from her. She’s as rich as a Jew, she can hand out five thousand at once, and she doesn’t turn up her nose at a pledge worth a rouble either. Lots of our fellows have been to her. Only she’s a terrible bitch...”

And he began to describe how spiteful she was, how capricious, how if you were a single day late with a pledge the thing was lost. She gave a quarter of what a thing was worth, and took five and even seven per cent a month in interest, and so on. The student chattered away and told him besides that the old woman had a sister, Lizaveta, whom she, so small and nasty as she was, beat every minute and kept in complete slavery, like a little child, though Lizaveta was at least six foot tall...
“There’s a phenomenon for you too!” cried the student, and roared with laughter.

They began to talk about Lizaveta. The student talked about her with a kind of special pleasure and kept laughing, and the officer listened with great interest and asked the student to send this Lizaveta to him to mend his linen. Raskolnikov did not miss a single word and learned everything at once: Lizaveta was the younger half-sister of the old woman (from different mothers), and she was already thirty-five. She worked for her sister day and night, served in the house as cook and laundress, and besides sewed for sale, even hired herself out to wash floors, and gave everything to her sister. She dared not take on any order or any work without the old woman’s permission. The old woman had already made her will, which Lizaveta herself knew, and by the will she was not to get a kopeck, except the movable property, the chairs and so on; all the money was left to a monastery in N. province, for the eternal repose of her soul. Lizaveta was of the tradesman class, not an official’s widow, unmarried, and terribly ungainly to look at, remarkably tall, with long, as if twisted, great feet, always in trodden-down goatskin shoes, and she kept herself clean. But what the student was most surprised at and laughed at was that Lizaveta was constantly pregnant...
“But you say she’s a fright?” the officer remarked.

“Yes, she’s so dark, like a soldier in disguise, but you know, she’s not a fright at all. She has such a kind face and eyes. Very much so. The proof is, lots of men like her. She’s so quiet, gentle, uncomplaining, willing, willing for anything. And her smile is really very nice.”
“So you like her too?” laughed the officer.
“For her strangeness. No, I’ll tell you what. I would kill that damned old woman and rob her, and I assure you, without the least prick of conscience,” the student added warmly.
The officer roared with laughter again, and Raskolnikov started. How strange it was!

“Wait, I want to ask you a serious question,” the student grew heated. “I was joking just now, of course, but look: on one side a stupid, senseless, worthless, spiteful, sick old woman, no use to anyone and, on the contrary, harmful to everyone, who does not know herself what she is living for, and who will die of herself tomorrow anyway. Do you understand? Do you understand?”
“Well, I understand,” answered the officer, staring attentively at his heated companion.

“Listen further. On the other side, young, fresh forces going to waste for lack of support, and that by the thousand, and that everywhere! A hundred, a thousand good deeds and undertakings that could be set up and put right with the old woman’s money, which is doomed to a monastery! Hundreds, perhaps thousands of lives put on the right road; dozens of families saved from destitution, from decay, from ruin, from depravity, from the venereal hospitals; and all with her money. Kill her and take her money, so as to devote yourself afterwards, with its help, to the service of all mankind and the common cause: what do you think, would not one tiny little crime be wiped out by thousands of good deeds? For one life, thousands of lives saved from rotting and decay. One death and a hundred lives in exchange: why, it’s arithmetic! And what does the life of this consumptive, stupid and spiteful old woman mean on the general scales? No more than the life of a louse, a cockroach, and not even that, because the old woman is harmful. She is eating up other people’s lives: the other day she bit Lizaveta’s finger out of spite; they nearly had to cut it off!”
“Of course she doesn’t deserve to live,” remarked the officer, “but there it is, it’s nature.”

“Eh, brother, but nature is corrected and guided, and without that we should drown in prejudices. Without that there would never have been a single great man. They say ‘duty, conscience’; I don’t want to say anything against duty and conscience; but how do we understand them? Wait, I’ll ask you another question. Listen!”
“No, you wait; I’ll ask you a question. Listen!”
“Well!”
“Here you are talking and making speeches, but tell me: will you kill the old woman yourself or not?”
“Of course not! I’m speaking of justice... It’s not a question of me...”
“Well, in my opinion, if you won’t dare do it yourself, then there’s no justice in it at all! Let’s have another game!”

Raskolnikov was in extraordinary agitation. Of course, all this was the most ordinary and most frequent young people’s talk and thought, which he had heard more than once already, only in other forms and on other subjects. But why should he have happened to hear precisely such talk and such thoughts just now, when exactly the same thoughts had just been born in his own head? And why, just now, as soon as he had carried away the germ of his thought from the old woman’s, should he hit precisely on a conversation about the old woman?.. This coincidence always seemed strange to him. This trivial tavern conversation had an extraordinary influence on him as the matter developed further: as if there really were some predestination here, some sign...

Coming back from the Haymarket, he threw himself on the sofa and sat for a whole hour without moving. Meanwhile it grew dark; he had no candle, and it did not even occur to him to light one. He could never remember whether he had been thinking about anything at that time. At last he felt the fever of earlier, the chill, and realised with pleasure that he could also lie down on the sofa. Soon a heavy, leaden sleep came down on him as if it were crushing him.

He slept an unusually long time and without dreams. Nastasya, who came in at ten o’clock the next morning, could hardly push him awake. She had brought him tea and bread. The tea was again used once already, and again in her own teapot.
“My, how he sleeps!” she cried indignantly. “He’s always asleep!”
He raised himself with an effort. His head ached; he stood up, turned round in his little room, and fell back on the sofa.
“Asleep again!” cried Nastasya. “Are you ill, or what?”
He made no answer.
“Do you want some tea?”
“Later,” he said with an effort, closing his eyes again and turning to the wall. Nastasya stood over him.
“Perhaps he really is ill,” she said, turned and went out.
She came in again at two o’clock with soup. He was lying as before. The tea stood untouched. Nastasya even took offence and began to push him angrily.
“Why are you snoring away!” she cried, looking at him with disgust. He raised himself and sat up, but said nothing to her and looked at the floor.
“Are you ill or not?” asked Nastasya, and again got no answer.
“You might at least go out into the street,” she said after a pause. “You might at least get some air. Are you going to eat, or what?”
“Later,” he said weakly. “Go away!” And he waved his hand.
She stood a little longer, looked at him with compassion, and went out.
A few minutes later he raised his eyes and looked for a long time at the tea and the soup. Then he took the bread, took the spoon and began to eat.

He ate a little, without appetite, three or four spoonfuls, as if mechanically. His head ached less. When he had eaten, he stretched out on the sofa again, but he could not sleep now; he lay without moving, face down, his face buried in the pillow. He kept dreaming, and they were such strange dreams: most often it seemed to him that he was somewhere in Africa, in Egypt, in some oasis. The caravan is resting, the camels lie quietly; palms grow all around in a whole circle; everyone is eating. But he keeps drinking water, straight from a stream which flows and murmurs right there beside him. And it is so cool, and the water is so wonderful, wonderfully blue, cold, running over stones of many colours and over such clean sand with golden sparkles... Suddenly he clearly heard a clock striking. He started, came to himself, raised his head, looked at the window, worked out the time, and suddenly jumped up, completely himself again, as if someone had torn him from the sofa. He went on tiptoe to the door, opened it softly a little way and began to listen down the stairs. His heart was beating terribly. But on the stairs everything was quiet, as if everyone were asleep... It seemed wild and strange to him that he could have slept in such oblivion since the day before and had done nothing yet, prepared nothing... And meanwhile perhaps it had struck six... And instead of sleep and stupor, an unusual, feverish and somehow bewildered bustle suddenly seized him. There were not many preparations, however. He strained every effort to think of everything and forget nothing; and his heart kept beating, thumping so that it became hard for him to breathe. First, he had to make a loop and sew it into his coat: a minute’s work. He reached under the pillow and found among the linen stuffed under it an old, unwashed shirt of his that was completely falling apart. From its rags he tore a strip about an inch and a half wide and fourteen inches long. He folded this strip in two, took off his wide, strong summer coat made of some thick cotton material (his only outer garment) and began to sew both ends of the strip under the left armpit on the inside. His hands shook as he sewed, but he managed it, and so that nothing could be seen from outside when he put the coat on again. The needle and thread had been ready for a long time and lay in the table drawer, in a piece of paper. As for the loop, it was a very clever invention of his own: the loop was meant for the axe. One could not carry an axe in one’s hands along the street. And if one hid it under one’s coat, one would still have to hold it with one’s hand, which would be noticeable. But now, with the loop, he had only to put the blade of the axe into it, and it would hang quietly, under his arm on the inside, all the way. And by putting his hand into the side pocket of his coat, he could hold the end of the axe handle too, so that it would not swing; and since the coat was very wide, a real sack, it could not be noticed from outside that he was holding something with his hand through the pocket. He had thought of this loop too, two weeks ago.

Having finished this, he pushed his fingers into a little crack between his “Turkish” sofa and the floor, felt about near the left corner and pulled out the pledge he had prepared long ago and hidden there. This pledge, however, was not a pledge at all, but simply a smoothly planed little piece of wood, no bigger or thicker than a silver cigarette case might be. He had found this piece of wood by chance on one of his walks, in a courtyard where there was some workshop in an outbuilding. Later he added to the piece of wood a smooth, thin strip of iron, probably broken off something, which he had also found in the street at the same time. Putting the two pieces together, of which the iron one was smaller than the wooden, he tied them together tightly, crosswise, with thread; then he wrapped them neatly and elegantly in clean white paper and tied it with thin tape, also crosswise, and arranged the knot so that it would be harder to untie. This was to distract the old woman’s attention for a while, when she began fiddling with the knot, and so to seize the moment. The iron plate had been added for weight, so that the old woman should not guess, at least at first, that the “thing” was wooden. All this had been kept under the sofa until the time came. He had only just taken out the pledge when suddenly someone shouted somewhere in the yard:
“It’s long past six!”
“Long past! My God!”

He rushed to the door, listened, seized his hat and began to go down his thirteen steps, carefully, soundlessly, like a cat. The most important thing lay ahead: to steal the axe from the kitchen. That the thing must be done with an axe he had decided long ago. He also had a folding garden knife; but he did not trust a knife, and especially not his own strength, and so he had settled finally on the axe. Let us note, by the way, one peculiarity of all the final decisions he had already made in this business. They had one strange property: the more final they became, the more hideous and absurd they at once became in his own eyes too. In spite of all his tormenting inner struggle, he could never, for a single moment, believe in the practicability of his plans, all this time.

And even if it had ever happened that everything had been worked out by him to the last point and finally decided, and no doubts of any kind remained, then, it seems, he would have given it all up as absurd, monstrous and impossible. But there still remained a whole abyss of unresolved points and doubts. As for where to get the axe, that trifle did not worry him at all, because nothing was easier. The point was that Nastasya, especially in the evenings, was constantly out: she would either run off to the neighbours or to the shop, and she always left the door wide open. That was the only thing the landlady quarrelled with her about. So he had only to go quietly into the kitchen when the time came and take the axe, and then, an hour later (when it was all over), go in and put it back. But doubts presented themselves too: suppose he came back an hour later to put it back, and there was Nastasya, back again. Of course he would have to walk past and wait until she went out again. But what if in the meantime she missed the axe, began to look for it, made an outcry: there was suspicion, or at least a reason for suspicion.

But these were still trifles, which he had not even begun to think about, and there was no time for them. He thought about the main thing, and put off the trifles until he had convinced himself about everything. But that seemed absolutely unattainable. So, at least, it seemed to him. He could not, for instance, imagine at all that he would one day finish thinking, get up and simply go there... Even his recent rehearsal (that is, the visit with the intention of finally looking over the place) he had only tried to make, and far from in earnest, but just like that: “Come, I’ll go and try it, why go on dreaming!” And at once he could not bear it, spat and ran away, furious with himself. And yet, it would seem, the whole analysis, in the sense of the moral resolution of the question, had already been finished by him: his casuistry had been sharpened like a razor, and he no longer found any conscious objections in himself. But in this last case he simply did not trust himself, and stubbornly, slavishly, searched for objections on all sides and by touch, as if someone were forcing him and drawing him to it. And the last day, which had come so unexpectedly and decided everything at once, acted on him almost entirely mechanically: as if someone had taken him by the hand and pulled him along, irresistibly, blindly, with unnatural force, without objections. As if he had caught a corner of his clothing in the wheel of a machine, and it had begun to draw him into it.

At first (long before, in fact) he had been occupied by one question: why are almost all crimes so easily detected and exposed, and why are the traces of almost all criminals so plainly marked? He came little by little to various and curious conclusions, and in his opinion the chief reason lay not so much in the material impossibility of hiding the crime as in the criminal himself: the criminal himself, almost every one, at the moment of the crime undergoes a kind of failure of will and reason, replaced, on the contrary, by a childish, phenomenal heedlessness, and precisely at the moment when reason and caution are most needed. By his conviction, it turned out that this eclipse of reason and failure of will take hold of a man like an illness, develop gradually, and reach their highest point shortly before the crime is committed; they continue in the same form at the very moment of the crime and for some time after it, depending on the individual; then they pass, as every illness passes. But the question whether the illness gives rise to the crime itself, or whether the crime itself, by some peculiarity of its nature, is always accompanied by something like an illness, he did not yet feel able to resolve.

Having reached such conclusions, he decided that with him personally, in his case, there could be no such sick upheavals, that his reason and will would remain with him, inalienably, all the time he was carrying out what he had planned, for the sole reason that what he had planned was “not a crime”... We pass over the whole process by which he arrived at this last decision; we have run too far ahead as it is... Let us only add that the actual, purely material difficulties of the business in general played a most secondary part in his mind. “One has only to keep all one’s will and all one’s reason over them, and they will all be overcome in their time, when one has to get to know all the details of the business down to the finest point...” But the business did not begin. He continued to believe least of all in his final decisions, and when the hour struck, everything turned out quite differently, as if by chance, even almost unexpectedly.

One most trivial circumstance stopped him dead before he was even down the stairs.
