As he came level with the landlady’s kitchen, open wide as always, he glanced cautiously into it, to see beforehand whether the landlady herself was there in Nastasya’s absence, and if not, whether the doors of her room were properly shut, so that she should not somehow look out from there when he went in for the axe. But what was his astonishment when he suddenly saw that Nastasya was not only at home this time, in her kitchen, but was even busy with work: taking linen out of a basket and hanging it on lines! Seeing him, she stopped hanging it, turned to him and looked at him the whole time he was passing. He turned his eyes away and walked past, as if noticing nothing. But it was all over: no axe! He was terribly struck.

“And what made me think,” he thought as he went down under the gateway, “what made me think that she would certainly not be at home at this moment? Why, why, why did I decide it so surely?” He was crushed, even somehow humiliated. He wanted to laugh at himself out of spite... A dull, brutal rage boiled up in him.

He stopped under the gateway, thinking. To go out into the street, just for appearances, to walk about, was loathsome to him; to go back home was more loathsome still. “And what a chance I have lost for ever!” he muttered, standing aimlessly under the gateway, right opposite the caretaker’s dark little room, which was also open. Suddenly he started. From the caretaker’s room, two steps away from him, from under the bench on the right, something gleamed in his eyes... He looked all around: no one. On tiptoe he went up to the caretaker’s room, went down two steps and called the caretaker in a weak voice. “Just so, he’s not in! Somewhere near, though, in the yard, because the door is wide open.” He rushed headlong at the axe (it was an axe) and pulled it out from under the bench, where it lay between two logs; right there, without going out, he fixed it in the loop, put both hands in his pockets and came out of the caretaker’s room; no one noticed! “If not reason, then the devil!” he thought, smiling strangely. This chance encouraged him extraordinarily.

He walked along quietly and sedately, without hurrying, so as not to give rise to any suspicion. He hardly looked at the passers-by, even tried not to look at faces at all and to be as inconspicuous as possible. Then he remembered his hat. “My God! And I had the money the day before yesterday, and I couldn’t change it for a cap!” A curse burst from his soul.

Glancing by chance, with one eye, into a little shop, he saw that by the clock on the wall it was already ten past seven. He had to hurry, and at the same time make a detour: come up to the house the long way round, from the other side...

Before, when he had happened to picture all this in his imagination, he had sometimes thought that he would be very afraid. But he was not very afraid now, even not afraid at all. At that moment he was even occupied by some irrelevant thoughts, only none of them for long. Passing the Yusupov Garden, he was even very much taken with the thought of building high fountains, and how well they would freshen the air in all the squares. Little by little he came to the conviction that if the Summer Garden were extended over the whole of the Field of Mars, and even joined to the garden of the Mikhailovsky Palace, it would be a splendid and most useful thing for the city. Then he was suddenly interested: why exactly, in all big cities, are people inclined, not simply from necessity but somehow particularly, to live and settle in precisely those parts of the city where there are no gardens and no fountains, where there is dirt and stench and every kind of filth? Then he remembered his own walks in the Haymarket, and for a moment he came to himself. “What nonsense,” he thought. “No, better not think about anything at all!”

“So, I suppose, those who are being led to execution fasten their thoughts on every object they meet on the way,” flashed through his head, but it only flashed like lightning; he himself quickly put out the thought... But now it was near, here was the house, here was the gateway. Somewhere a clock suddenly struck once. “What, can it be half past seven? It can’t be; it must be fast!”

Luckily for him, all went well again at the gateway. More than that, as if on purpose, at that very moment a huge load of hay had just driven in at the gate in front of him, completely screening him all the time he was passing under the archway, and as soon as the load had driven through the gateway into the yard, he slipped instantly to the right. There, on the other side of the load, several voices could be heard shouting and arguing, but no one noticed him and no one came towards him. Many windows looking onto that huge square courtyard were open at that moment, but he did not raise his head: he had not the strength. The staircase to the old woman’s was near, straight from the gateway on the right. He was already on the stairs...

Getting his breath and pressing his hand on his thumping heart, at the same time feeling for the axe and setting it straight once more, he began to climb the stairs carefully and quietly, listening every moment. But the staircase too was quite empty at that hour; all the doors were shut; he met no one. On the second floor one empty flat, it is true, stood wide open, and painters were working in it, but they did not even look. He stood still, thought, and went on. “Of course, it would be better if they were not here at all, but... there are two floors more above them.”

But here was the fourth floor, here was the door, here was the flat opposite; the empty one. On the third floor, by every sign, the flat directly under the old woman’s was empty too: the visiting card nailed to the door with little nails had been taken down: they had moved out!.. He was gasping for breath. For one instant the thought flashed through his mind: “Shouldn’t I go away?” But he gave himself no answer and began to listen at the old woman’s flat: a dead silence. Then he listened once more down the stairs, listened long and attentively... Then he looked round for the last time, pulled himself together, set himself straight and once more tried the axe in the loop. “Am I not pale... very?” he thought. “Am I not especially agitated? She is distrustful... Shouldn’t I wait a little longer... until my heart stops?..”

But his heart did not stop. On the contrary, as if on purpose, it beat harder, harder, harder... He could not bear it; he slowly stretched out his hand to the bell and rang. Half a minute later he rang again, louder.

No answer. There was no point in ringing for nothing, and it did not suit him either. The old woman, of course, was at home, but she was suspicious and alone. He knew her habits in part... and once more he put his ear close to the door. Whether his senses were so sharpened (which is hard to suppose in general), or whether it really was very audible, he suddenly made out something like a cautious rustle of a hand at the door handle and something like the rustle of a dress against the door itself. Someone was standing unnoticed right by the lock and, exactly as he was here outside, was listening, hiding inside and, it seemed, also with an ear pressed to the door...

He stirred on purpose and muttered something rather loudly, so as not to give any sign that he was hiding; then he rang a third time, but quietly, solidly and without any impatience. Remembering this afterwards, brightly, clearly (this minute was stamped on him for ever), he could not understand where he had got so much cunning, all the more since his mind seemed to grow dim for moments, and he hardly felt his body on him at all... A moment later he heard the bolt being drawn back.
## CHAPTER VII
The door, as before, opened a tiny crack, and again two sharp, distrustful eyes stared at him out of the darkness. Here Raskolnikov lost his head and almost made a serious mistake.

Afraid that the old woman would be frightened at their being alone, and not hoping that his appearance would reassure her, he took hold of the door and pulled it towards him, so that the old woman should not somehow take it into her head to lock herself in again. Seeing this, she did not pull the door back towards her, but she did not let go of the handle either, so that he almost pulled her out onto the landing together with the door. Seeing that she was standing across the doorway and would not let him pass, he walked straight at her. She sprang back in fright, was about to say something, but seemed unable to, and stared at him wide-eyed.

“Good evening, Alyona Ivanovna,” he began, as casually as he could, but his voice would not obey him; it broke off and trembled. “I have... brought you a thing... but let us come over here... to the light...” And leaving her, he walked straight into the room without being asked. The old woman ran after him; her tongue was loosened.
“Lord! What do you want?.. Who are you? What do you want?”
“Excuse me, Alyona Ivanovna... you know me... Raskolnikov... here, I have brought the pledge I promised the other day...” And he held the pledge out to her.

The old woman glanced at the pledge, but at once fixed her eyes straight on the eyes of her uninvited visitor. She looked attentively, spitefully and distrustfully. A minute passed; he even thought he saw something like mockery in her eyes, as if she had already guessed everything. He felt that he was losing his head, that he was almost afraid, so afraid that it seemed to him that if she went on looking like that and did not say a word for another half minute, he would have run away from her.
“Why do you look at me like that, as if you did not recognise me?” he said suddenly, also with spite. “Take it if you want it, and if not I will go to someone else; I have no time.”
He had not even meant to say this; it simply came out of itself.
The old woman came to herself, and her visitor’s resolute tone evidently reassured her.
“But why so sudden, my dear... what is it?” she asked, looking at the pledge.
“A silver cigarette case: I told you last time.”
She held out her hand.
“But why are you so pale? Your hands are trembling too! Have you been bathing, my dear?”

“Fever,” he answered abruptly. “One can’t help being pale... when one has nothing to eat,” he added, hardly able to get the words out. His strength was leaving him again. But the answer seemed plausible; the old woman took the pledge.
“What is it?” she asked, looking Raskolnikov over intently once more and weighing the pledge in her hand.
“A thing... a cigarette case... silver... look.”
“But it doesn’t seem to be silver... My, how he has wrapped it up.”

Trying to untie the string and turning to the window, to the light (all her windows were shut, in spite of the stuffiness), she left him completely for a few seconds and stood with her back to him. He unbuttoned his coat and freed the axe from the loop, but did not take it out altogether yet; he only held it with his right hand under his clothes. His hands were terribly weak; he could feel them himself growing more and more numb and wooden with every moment. He was afraid he would let go of the axe and drop it... suddenly his head seemed to spin.
“What has he wrapped up here!” the old woman cried in annoyance, and moved towards him.

Not another moment could be lost. He took the axe right out, swung it up with both hands, hardly aware of himself, and almost without effort, almost mechanically, brought the butt of it down on her head. It was as if he had no strength. But as soon as he had once brought the axe down, the strength was born in him.

The old woman, as always, had nothing on her head. Her thin, fair hair, streaked with grey and thickly greased as usual, was plaited into a rat’s tail and pinned up under a broken horn comb that stuck out at the back of her head. The blow fell right on the crown of her head, which her small height made easier. She cried out, but very faintly, and suddenly sank all the way to the floor, though she still managed to raise both hands to her head. In one hand she still went on holding the “pledge”. Then he struck her with all his strength once and again, still with the butt and still on the crown. The blood gushed out as if from an overturned glass, and the body fell over on its back. He stepped back, let it fall, and at once bent down to her face; she was already dead. Her eyes were wide open, as if they wanted to jump out, and her forehead and her whole face were wrinkled and distorted by a spasm.

He put the axe on the floor beside the dead woman and at once reached into her pocket, trying not to stain himself with the flowing blood: the same right-hand pocket from which she had taken her keys last time. He was in full possession of his mind; there were no more blackouts or dizziness, but his hands were still trembling. He remembered afterwards that he had even been very attentive and careful, and kept trying not to get stained... He took out the keys at once; they were all, as before, in one bunch, on one steel ring. He ran with them at once into the bedroom. It was a very small room, with an enormous case of icons. Against another wall stood a big bed, very clean, with a silk patchwork quilt filled with wadding. Against the third wall was the chest of drawers. A strange thing: as soon as he began fitting the keys to the chest of drawers, as soon as he heard them jingle, a kind of convulsion seemed to pass through him. He suddenly wanted again to drop everything and go away. But that was only for a moment; it was too late to go away. He even smiled at himself, when suddenly another anxious thought struck him. It suddenly seemed to him that the old woman might still be alive and might still come to. Dropping the keys and the chest of drawers, he ran back to the body, seized the axe and swung it up once more over the old woman, but did not bring it down. There was no doubt that she was dead. Bending down and examining her more closely again, he saw clearly that the skull was smashed and even twisted a little to one side. He was about to feel it with his finger, but he snatched his hand back; it could be seen without that. Meanwhile a whole pool of blood had already flowed out. Suddenly he noticed a cord round her neck; he tugged at it, but the cord was strong and would not break; besides, it was soaked in blood. He tried to pull it out like that, from her bosom, but something was in the way, caught. In his impatience he raised the axe again to cut the cord right there, on the body, from above, but he did not dare, and with difficulty, smearing his hands and the axe, after two minutes’ fumbling, he cut the cord without touching the body with the axe, and took it off; he had not been mistaken: a purse. On the cord were two crosses, one of cypress wood and one of copper, and besides them an enamelled little icon; and hanging there with them was a small, greasy chamois-leather purse with a steel rim and ring. The purse was stuffed very full; Raskolnikov thrust it into his pocket without looking at it, threw the crosses on the old woman’s breast, and, taking the axe with him this time, rushed back into the bedroom.

He was in a terrible hurry; he seized the keys and began fumbling with them again. But somehow nothing went right: they would not go into the locks. It was not that his hands were trembling so much, but he kept making mistakes: he would see, for instance, that a key was the wrong one, that it did not fit, and still he kept pushing it in. Suddenly he remembered and realised that the big key with the notched bit, which was dangling there with the other little ones, could certainly not be for the chest of drawers at all (as had occurred to him last time too), but for some trunk, and that perhaps everything was hidden in that trunk. He left the chest of drawers and at once crawled under the bed, knowing that old women usually keep their trunks under their beds. Just so: there stood a sizeable trunk, more than a yard long, with a rounded lid, covered in red morocco and studded with steel nails. The notched key fitted exactly and opened it. On top, under a white sheet, lay a hareskin coat covered with red brocade; under it was a silk dress, then a shawl, and further down, it seemed, there was nothing but rags. First of all he began to wipe his bloodstained hands on the red brocade. “It’s red, and on red blood is less noticeable,” he reasoned, and suddenly he came to himself: “Lord! Am I going out of my mind?” he thought in fright.

But as soon as he stirred these rags, a gold watch suddenly slipped out from under the coat. He rushed to turn everything over. Indeed, gold things were mixed in among the rags, probably all pledges, redeemed and unredeemed: bracelets, chains, earrings, pins and so on. Some were in cases, others simply wrapped in newspaper, but neatly and carefully, in double sheets, and tied round with tape. Without the least delay he began stuffing his trouser pockets and his coat pockets with them, without sorting them or opening the packets and cases; but he did not have time to take many...

Suddenly he heard someone walking in the room where the old woman was. He stopped and kept still as a dead man. But all was quiet, so he must have imagined it. Suddenly he distinctly heard a faint cry, or as if someone had moaned softly and abruptly and fallen silent. Then again dead silence, for a minute or two. He sat crouching by the trunk and waited, hardly drawing breath, but suddenly he jumped up, seized the axe and ran out of the bedroom.

In the middle of the room stood Lizaveta, with a big bundle in her hands, gazing in a stupor at her murdered sister, as white as a sheet and as if unable to cry out. Seeing him run out, she trembled like a leaf, with a fine trembling, and spasms ran all over her face; she half raised her hand, opened her mouth, but still did not cry out, and slowly, backwards, began to move away from him into the corner, staring intently, point-blank, at him, but still not crying out, as if she had not enough air to cry out. He rushed at her with the axe; her lips were twisted so pitifully, like those of very small children when they begin to be frightened of something, stare at the thing that frightens them, and are about to scream. And this unhappy Lizaveta was so simple, so downtrodden and so frightened once and for all, that she did not even raise a hand to protect her face, though that was the most necessary and natural gesture at that moment, because the axe was raised right over her face. She only lifted her free left hand a very little, far short of her face, and slowly stretched it out towards him, as if to push him away. The blow fell right on her skull, with the blade, and at once split the whole upper part of her forehead, almost to the crown. She simply crashed down. Raskolnikov completely lost his head; he seized her bundle, threw it down again, and ran into the hall.

Fear was taking hold of him more and more, especially after this second, completely unexpected murder. He wanted to run away from here as fast as possible. And if at that moment he had been able to see and reason more clearly; if only he could have grasped all the difficulties of his position, all its despair, all its hideousness and absurdity, and understood at the same time how many obstacles, and perhaps even crimes, still remained for him to overcome and commit in order to get out of here and reach home, then it is very possible that he would have thrown up everything and at once gone to give himself up, and not even from fear for himself, but simply from horror and disgust at what he had done. The disgust especially rose and grew in him with every minute. Not for anything in the world would he have gone back to the trunk now, or even into the rooms.

But a kind of absent-mindedness, as if even a kind of reverie, began little by little to take hold of him: at moments he seemed to forget himself, or rather to forget the main thing, and to cling to trifles. However, glancing into the kitchen and seeing a bucket half full of water on a bench, he thought of washing his hands and the axe. His hands were covered in blood and sticky. He put the axe blade down straight into the water, seized a bit of soap that lay on the window sill on a cracked saucer, and began to wash his hands right there in the bucket. When he had washed them, he took out the axe too, washed the iron, and for a long time, about three minutes, washed the wood where it was bloodstained, even trying the blood with soap. Then he wiped it all with some linen that was drying there on a line stretched across the kitchen, and then for a long time, attentively, examined the axe at the window. There were no traces left; only the handle was still damp. He carefully put the axe into the loop, under his coat. Then, as far as the light in the dim kitchen allowed, he examined his coat, his trousers, his boots. On the outside, at first glance, there seemed to be nothing; only there were stains on his boots. He wetted a rag and wiped his boots. He knew, however, that he was not looking properly, that perhaps there was something that would catch the eye which he was not noticing. He stood thinking in the middle of the room. A tormenting, dark thought rose in him: the thought that he was going mad, and that at this moment he was unable either to reason or to protect himself, that perhaps he ought not to be doing at all what he was doing now... “My God! I must run, run!” he muttered, and rushed into the hall. But there such a horror awaited him as he had certainly never experienced before.

He stood, looked, and did not believe his eyes: the door, the outer door, from the hall to the stairs, the very door at which he had rung and come in a little while ago, stood unlocked, even open a whole hand’s breadth: neither locked nor bolted, all the time, all this time! The old woman had not locked it after him, perhaps out of caution. But God! He had seen Lizaveta afterwards! And how could he, how could he not have guessed that she must have come in from somewhere! Not through the wall.
He rushed to the door and put the bolt on.
“But no, that’s wrong again! I must go, go...”
He took off the bolt, opened the door and began listening on the stairs.

He listened for a long time. Somewhere far away, below, probably under the gateway, two voices were shouting loudly and shrilly, arguing and swearing. “What are they doing?..” He waited patiently. At last everything fell silent at once, as if cut off; they had gone their ways. He was about to go out, when suddenly on the floor below a door onto the stairs was flung open noisily, and someone began going down, humming a tune. “How they all make such a noise!” flashed through his head. He shut the door behind him again and waited. At last everything was silent, not a soul. He had already taken a step onto the stairs when suddenly again someone’s new footsteps were heard.

These steps sounded very far off, still at the very bottom of the stairs, but he remembered very well and distinctly that from the very first sound he had begun for some reason to suspect that they were certainly coming here, to the fourth floor, to the old woman’s. Why? Were the sounds so special, so significant? The steps were heavy, even, unhurried. Now he had passed the first floor, now he had climbed further; louder and louder! The heavy panting of the man coming up could be heard. Now the third floor had begun... Here! And suddenly it seemed to him that he had turned to stone, that it was just like a dream when one dreams that someone is chasing one, is near, wants to kill one, and one is rooted to the spot and cannot even move one’s arms.

And at last, when the visitor had already begun to climb to the fourth floor, only then did he suddenly start all over and managed after all to slip back quickly and deftly from the landing into the flat and shut the door behind him. Then he seized the bolt and quietly, soundlessly, slipped it into the catch. Instinct helped him. When he had done it all, he hid without breathing, right by the door. The uninvited visitor was at the door too. They stood now facing each other, as he and the old woman had a little while before, when the door separated them and he was listening.

The visitor panted heavily several times. “Fat and big, he must be,” thought Raskolnikov, gripping the axe in his hand. Indeed, it was exactly as if he were dreaming all this. The visitor seized the bell and rang hard.

As soon as the tinny sound of the bell jangled, it suddenly seemed to him that something stirred in the room. For a few seconds he even listened seriously. The stranger rang once more, waited again, and suddenly, impatiently, began tugging at the door handle with all his might. Raskolnikov watched in horror the hook of the bolt jumping in its catch, and with dull fear waited for the bolt to jump out any moment. Indeed, it seemed possible: they were tugging so hard. He thought of holding the bolt with his hand, but the man might guess. His head seemed to be beginning to spin again. “I shall fall!” flashed through him, but the stranger began to speak, and he came to himself at once.

“What are they doing in there, snoring, or has someone strangled them? Thrrrice-cursed women!” he bellowed as if from a barrel. “Hey, Alyona Ivanovna, you old witch! Lizaveta Ivanovna, you indescribable beauty! Open up! Ugh, curse them, are they asleep, or what?”
And again, in a fury, he pulled the bell ten times running with all his might. He was certainly a man of authority and on familiar terms in the house.
At that very moment light, hurried steps were suddenly heard not far off on the stairs. Someone else was coming up. Raskolnikov did not hear him at first.
“Is there really no one there?” the newcomer called out in a ringing, cheerful voice, addressing the first visitor directly, who was still tugging at the bell. “Good evening, Koch!”
“From his voice, he must be very young,” Raskolnikov suddenly thought.
“The devil knows what’s going on; I’ve almost broken the lock,” answered Koch. “But how do you know me?”
“Well, really! Why, the day before yesterday at the Gambrinus I took three games running off you at billiards!”
“So they’re not in? Strange. Terribly stupid, though. Where could the old woman have gone? I have business with her.”
“And so have I, my dear fellow, business!”
“Well, what can we do? We’ll have to go back. Eh-eh! And I was hoping to get some money!” cried the young man.

“Of course, go back; but why make an appointment? She fixed the time herself, the witch. It’s out of my way, too. And where the devil should she go traipsing about, I don’t understand? The witch sits there all year round going sour, her legs ache, and then suddenly she’s off on an outing!”
“Shouldn’t we ask the caretaker?”
“Ask what?”
“Where she has gone and when she’ll be back?”
“Hm... devil... ask... But she never goes anywhere...” And he tugged at the door handle once more. “Devil, nothing to be done, we’ll have to go!”
“Wait!” the young man suddenly cried. “Look: do you see how the door gives when you pull it?”
“Well?”
“That means it isn’t locked, it’s bolted, on the hook, that is! Do you hear the bolt rattle?”
“Well?”

“Why, don’t you understand? That means one of them is at home. If they had all gone out, they would have locked it with a key from outside, not bolted it from inside. But here... do you hear the bolt rattle? And to bolt the door from inside, you have to be at home, do you understand? So they are at home, but they won’t open!”
“Bah! Why, so it is!” cried the astonished Koch. “So what are they doing in there!” And he began tugging at the door furiously.
“Wait!” the young man cried again. “Don’t pull at it! There’s something wrong here... you rang, you pulled, and they don’t open; that means either they have both fainted, or...”
“What?”
“I’ll tell you what: let’s go for the caretaker; let him wake them himself.”
“Good idea!” Both started down.
“Wait! You stay here, and I’ll run down for the caretaker.”
“Why should I stay?”
“Well, you never know?..”
“All right...”
“I’m training to be an examining magistrate, you know! There is obviously, ob-vi-ous-ly something wrong here!” the young man cried hotly, and ran off down the stairs.

Koch stayed, moved the bell once more, softly, and it gave one jangle; then quietly, as if reflecting and examining, he began to move the door handle, pulling it towards him and letting it go, to make sure once more that it was only bolted. Then, puffing, he bent down and began looking through the keyhole; but the key was in it on the inside, so nothing could be seen.

Raskolnikov stood gripping the axe. He was as if in delirium. He was even preparing to fight them when they came in. While they were knocking and talking it over, the thought had suddenly come to him several times to finish it all at once and shout to them through the door. At times he wanted to begin swearing at them, teasing them, until they opened the door. “If only it would be soon!” flashed through his head.
“But he, devil take it...”
Time passed, a minute, another; no one came. Koch began to fidget.
“Devil take it, though!..” he suddenly shouted, and, impatient, abandoned his watch and went down too, hurrying and stamping down the stairs in his boots. The steps died away.
“Lord, what am I to do!”

Raskolnikov took off the bolt and opened the door a little: nothing could be heard; and suddenly, no longer thinking at all, he went out, shut the door behind him as tightly as he could, and set off downstairs.
He had already gone down three flights when suddenly there was a loud noise below: where could he go! There was nowhere to hide. He started to run back, into the flat again.
“Hey, you devil, damn you! Stop him!”
With a shout someone burst out of some flat below and not so much ran as fell down the stairs, shouting at the top of his voice:
“Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! The devil take you-ou-ou!”

The shout ended in a shriek; the last sounds were already heard from the yard; everything fell silent. But at that same moment several men, talking loudly and fast, began to come noisily up the stairs. There were three or four of them. He made out the young man’s ringing voice. “It’s them!”

In utter despair he went straight down to meet them: come what may! If they stop me, all is lost; if they let me pass, all is lost too: they will remember me. They were already drawing near; only one flight was left between them, and suddenly, salvation! A few steps from him, on the right, an empty flat, wide open, the same flat on the second floor where the workmen had been painting, and now, as if on purpose, they had gone. It must have been they who had just run out with such shouting. The floors had just been painted; in the middle of the room stood a little tub and a crock with paint and a brush. In an instant he slipped through the open door and hid behind the wall, and just in time: they were already standing on the landing. Then they turned upward and went past, to the fourth floor, talking loudly. He waited, came out on tiptoe and ran downstairs.
No one on the stairs! Nor under the gateway. He walked quickly through the archway and turned left along the street.

He knew very well, he knew perfectly well that at that moment they were already in the flat, that they had been very surprised to find it unlocked when it had been locked just before, that they were already looking at the bodies, and that not more than a minute would pass before they guessed and fully understood that the murderer had only just been there and had managed to hide somewhere, slip past them, and run away; perhaps they would even guess that he had been sitting in the empty flat while they went up. And yet on no account did he dare quicken his pace much, though there were still about a hundred paces to the first turning. “Shouldn’t I slip into some gateway and wait somewhere on a strange staircase? No, disaster! Shouldn’t I throw the axe away somewhere? Shouldn’t I take a cab? Disaster! Disaster!”

At last here was the lane; he turned into it half dead; here he was already half saved, and he knew it: less suspicion, and besides, there were a lot of people bustling about here, and he was lost among them like a grain of sand. But all these torments had so weakened him that he could hardly move. Sweat was pouring off him in drops; his neck was all wet. “Look at him, he’s had a skinful!” someone shouted at him when he came out onto the canal.

He hardly remembered himself now; the further he went, the worse it was. He remembered, however, how suddenly, coming out onto the canal, he was frightened that there were few people there and that he would be more noticeable, and wanted to turn back into the lane. Although he was almost falling, he still made a detour and came home from quite another side.

He was not fully conscious as he went through the gateway of his house either; at least he was already on the stairs before he remembered the axe. And yet a very important task lay before him: to put it back, and as unnoticeably as possible. Of course, he was no longer able to realise that it might perhaps have been much better for him not to put the axe back in its old place at all, but to throw it, even later, into some strange yard.

But it all went off well. The door of the caretaker’s room was shut, but not locked, so it was most likely that the caretaker was in. But he had so lost the ability to think anything out that he went straight up to the caretaker’s room and opened the door. If the caretaker had asked him, “What do you want?”, he might perhaps simply have handed him the axe. But again the caretaker was not there, and he managed to put the axe back in its old place under the bench; he even covered it with a log as before. He met no one, not a single soul, after that all the way to his room; the landlady’s door was shut. Going into his room, he threw himself on the sofa just as he was. He did not sleep, but he was in a kind of trance. If anyone had come into his room then, he would have jumped up at once and screamed. Scraps and fragments of thoughts swarmed in his head; but he could not catch hold of a single one, could not stop at a single one, in spite of all his efforts...
## PART II · CHAPTER I

He lay like that for a very long time. Sometimes he seemed to wake up, and at those moments he noticed that it had long been night, but it did not occur to him to get up. At last he noticed that it was already light as day. He was lying on his back on the sofa, still stunned from his recent trance. Terrible, desperate screams came sharply to him from the street, which, however, he heard every night under his window at about three o’clock. It was they that had woken him now. “Ah! There are the drunks coming out of the taverns,” he thought. “It’s three o’clock,” and suddenly he jumped up as if someone had torn him from the sofa. “What! Three o’clock already!” He sat on the sofa, and then he remembered everything! Suddenly, in one moment, he remembered everything!

For the first moment he thought he would go mad. A terrible cold gripped him; but the cold came also from the fever, which had started in him long before, while he slept. Now suddenly such a shivering fit struck him that his teeth almost jumped out, and everything in him shook. He opened the door and began to listen: in the house everything was fast asleep. In amazement he looked at himself and at everything in the room around him, and did not understand: how could he have come in yesterday and not fastened the door on the hook, and thrown himself on the sofa, not only without undressing, but even with his hat on: it had rolled off and lay right there on the floor, near the pillow. “If anyone had come in, what would he have thought? That I was drunk, but...” He rushed to the window. There was enough light, and he quickly began to examine himself, all over, from head to foot, all his clothes: were there any traces? But that would not do: shaking with the chill, he began to take everything off and examine it all again. He turned everything over, to the last thread and scrap, and, not trusting himself, repeated the examination three times. But there was nothing, it seemed, no traces; only in the place where the bottoms of his trousers were frayed and hung in a fringe, there were thick traces of dried blood on that fringe. He seized his big folding knife and cut off the fringe. There seemed to be nothing else. Suddenly he remembered that the purse and the things he had taken out of the old woman’s trunk were all still in his pockets! He had not even thought until now of taking them out and hiding them! He had not remembered them even now, as he examined his clothes! What was this? In an instant he rushed to take them out and throw them on the table. When he had taken out everything, even turned his pockets inside out to make sure nothing was left, he carried the whole pile into the corner. There, in the very corner, low down, the wallpaper, which had come away from the wall, was torn in one place: at once he began stuffing everything into this hole, under the paper: “It’s gone in! Everything out of sight, and the purse too!” he thought joyfully, half rising and staring dully at the corner, at the hole, which bulged out still more. Suddenly he shuddered all over with horror: “My God,” he whispered in despair, “what is the matter with me? Is that hidden? Is that how one hides things?”

It is true that he had not reckoned on things; he had thought there would be only money, and so he had not prepared a place beforehand. “But now, now what am I glad about?” he thought. “Is that how one hides things? Truly my reason is leaving me!” In exhaustion he sat down on the sofa, and at once an unbearable chill shook him again. Mechanically he pulled over him his old student’s winter coat, which lay beside him on a chair, warm but almost in rags by now, and sleep and delirium seized him again at once. He sank into oblivion.

Not more than five minutes later he jumped up again and at once, in a frenzy, rushed to his clothes again. “How could I fall asleep again, when nothing has been done! Just so, just so: I still haven’t taken off the loop under the arm! I forgot, forgot such a thing! Such a piece of evidence!” He tore off the loop and quickly began tearing it into pieces, stuffing them under the pillow among the linen. “Pieces of torn linen will not rouse suspicion in any case; it seems so, it seems so!” he repeated, standing in the middle of the room, and with attention strained to the point of pain he began looking all around again, on the floor and everywhere, to see whether he had forgotten anything else. The certainty that everything, even memory, even simple reasoning, was leaving him began to torment him unbearably. “What, can it be beginning already, can this be the punishment coming already? There, there, just so!” Indeed, the bits of fringe he had cut off his trousers were lying right on the floor, in the middle of the room, for the first comer to see! “But what is the matter with me!” he cried again, as if lost.

Then a strange thought came into his head: that perhaps all his clothes were covered in blood, that perhaps there were many stains, but he simply did not see them, did not notice them, because his reasoning was weakened, shattered... his mind darkened... Suddenly he remembered that there had been blood on the purse too. “Bah! Then there must be blood in the pocket too, because I put the purse in my pocket still wet!” In an instant he turned the pocket inside out, and, just so, there were traces on the lining of the pocket, stains! “So my reason has not quite left me yet, so I still have some reasoning and memory, since I realised it and guessed it myself!” he thought triumphantly, drawing a deep and joyful breath with his whole chest. “It is simply the weakness of fever, delirium for a moment,” and he tore out the whole lining of the left trouser pocket. At that moment a ray of sunshine lit up his left boot: on the sock, which peeped out of the boot, there seemed to be marks. He threw off the boot: “Marks indeed! The whole tip of the sock is soaked in blood”; he must have stepped carelessly in that pool then... “But what am I to do with this now? Where am I to put this sock, the fringe, the pocket?”

He gathered it all up in his hand and stood in the middle of the room. “In the stove? But they will start rummaging in the stove first of all. Burn it? But burn it with what? I haven’t even any matches. No, better to go out somewhere and throw it all away. Yes! Better throw it away!” he repeated, sitting down on the sofa again, “and at once, this minute, without delay!..” But instead his head sank on the pillow again; again an unbearable chill froze him; again he pulled the coat over himself. And for a long time, several hours, he kept imagining in fits and starts that “now, at once, without putting it off, I ought to go somewhere and throw it all away, to get it out of sight, quickly, quickly!” Several times he made a dash to get up from the sofa, tried to stand, but by now he could not. What finally woke him was a loud knocking at the door.

“Open up, are you alive or not? He’s always snoring!” shouted Nastasya, banging on the door with her fist. “Snoring the whole day long like a dog! A dog is what he is! Open up, will you. It’s past ten.”
“Maybe he isn’t in!” said a man’s voice.
“Bah! That is the caretaker’s voice... What does he want?”
He jumped up and sat on the sofa. His heart was beating so hard that it even hurt.
“And who put the hook on, then?” objected Nastasya. “Look at him, he’s started locking himself in! Is he afraid he’ll be carried off? Open up, you blockhead, wake up!”
“What do they want? Why the caretaker? Everything is known. Resist or open? Let it all go...”
He half rose, leaned forward and took off the hook.
His whole room was so small that he could take off the hook without getting up from the bed.
Just so: there stood the caretaker and Nastasya.
Nastasya looked him over somehow strangely. He glanced at the caretaker with a defiant and desperate look. The man silently held out to him a grey paper folded in two and sealed with bottle wax.
“A summons, from the police office,” he said, handing him the paper.
“From what office?..”
“The police, that is, they’re calling you, to the office. You know what office.”
“To the police!.. What for?..”
“How should I know? They want you, so go.” He looked at him attentively, looked around and turned to go.

“He seems to have fallen properly ill, hasn’t he?” remarked Nastasya, who had not taken her eyes off him. The caretaker too turned his head for a moment. “He’s been in a fever since yesterday,” she added.
He did not answer and held the paper in his hands without opening it.
“Don’t get up, then,” Nastasya went on, moved to pity and seeing that he was lowering his feet from the sofa. “If you’re ill, don’t go: it won’t burn down. What have you got in your hands?”

He looked: in his right hand he had the cut-off pieces of fringe, the sock and the scraps of the torn-out pocket. He had slept with them like that. Afterwards, thinking about it, he remembered that even half waking in his fever he had gripped all this tight in his hand and fallen asleep again like that.

“Look what rags he has collected, and he sleeps with them as if they were treasure...” And Nastasya went off into her sickly, nervous laugh. In an instant he thrust everything under his coat and fixed his eyes on her intently. Though he could understand very little clearly at that moment, he felt that a man would not be treated like that when they came to arrest him. “But... the police?”
“Would you have some tea? Do you want some? I’ll bring it; there’s some left...”
“No... I’ll go: I’ll go right now,” he muttered, getting to his feet.
“You won’t even get down the stairs, I bet?”
“I’ll go...”
“As you like.”

She went out after the caretaker. At once he rushed to the light to examine the sock and the fringe: “There are stains, but not very noticeable; it is all dirty, rubbed and faded already. Anyone who doesn’t know beforehand won’t make anything out. So Nastasya could not have noticed anything from a distance, thank God!” Then, trembling, he opened the summons and began to read; he read for a long time and at last he understood. It was an ordinary summons from the district police to appear that very day, at half past nine, at the office of the district superintendent.

“But when has this ever happened? I have no business of my own with the police! And why just today?” he thought in tormenting bewilderment. “Lord, let it be over quickly!” He was about to throw himself on his knees to pray, but he even laughed himself, not at the prayer but at himself. He hastily began to dress. “If I am lost, I am lost; it’s all the same! Put on the sock!” he suddenly thought. “It will get still more rubbed in the dust, and the traces will disappear.” But no sooner had he put it on than he pulled it off again with disgust and horror. He pulled it off, but, realising that he had no other, he took it and put it on again, and again he laughed. “All this is conventional, all relative, all this is merely forms,” he thought fleetingly, with only the very edge of his mind, while he himself was trembling all over. “There, I have put it on! I ended by putting it on after all!” The laughter, however, was at once replaced by despair. “No, it is beyond my strength...” he thought. His legs were trembling. “From fear,” he muttered to himself. His head was spinning and aching from the fever. “It’s a trick! They want to lure me by a trick and then suddenly trip me up on everything,” he went on to himself as he went out onto the stairs. “The bad thing is that I am almost delirious... I may blurt out some stupid lie...”

On the stairs he remembered that he was leaving all the things just like that, in the hole in the wallpaper: “and perhaps they will search on purpose while I am out,” he remembered, and stopped. But such despair and, if one may say so, such a cynicism of ruin suddenly took hold of him that he waved his hand and went on.
“If only it would be quick!..”

In the street the heat was unbearable again; not a drop of rain all these days. Again dust, bricks and lime, again the stench from the shops and taverns, again drunks every minute, Finnish pedlars and half-broken-down cabs. The sun flashed brightly in his eyes, so that it hurt to look and his head spun completely: the usual sensation of a man in a fever who suddenly comes out into the street on a bright, sunny day.
When he reached the turning into yesterday’s street, he glanced down it with tormenting anxiety, at that house... and at once looked away.
“If they ask, perhaps I’ll tell,” he thought, as he came near the police office.

The office was about a quarter of a verst from his lodging. It had only just moved to new premises, in a new building, on the fourth floor. He had been in the old premises once, briefly, but a very long time ago. Going in under the gateway, he saw on the right a staircase, down which a peasant was coming with a book in his hands: “a caretaker, then; so this is where the office is,” and he began to climb at random. He did not want to ask anyone anything.
“I’ll go in, fall on my knees and tell everything...” he thought, as he came up to the fourth floor.

The staircase was narrow, steep and all covered in slops. All the kitchens of all the flats on all four floors opened onto this staircase and stood open like that almost all day. Because of that it was terribly stuffy. Caretakers with books under their arms, messengers and various people of both sexes, visitors, went up and down. The door into the office itself was also wide open. He went in and stopped in the entrance room. Some peasants were standing there waiting. Here too the stuffiness was extreme, and besides there was a sickening smell of fresh paint, not yet dry, made with rancid oil, in the newly painted rooms. After waiting a little, he decided to move on into the next room. The rooms were all tiny and low. A terrible impatience drew him on and on. No one noticed him. In the second room some clerks were sitting and writing, dressed perhaps a little better than he was, all strange-looking people. He turned to one of them.
“What do you want?”
He showed the summons from the office.
“You are a student?” the man asked, glancing at the summons.
“Yes, a former student.”
The clerk looked him over, though without any curiosity. He was a particularly dishevelled man with a fixed idea in his look.
“There is nothing to be learned from this one, because it is all the same to him,” thought Raskolnikov.
“Go in there, to the chief clerk,” said the clerk, and jabbed his finger forward, pointing to the very last room.

He went into that room (the fourth in order), cramped and packed full of people, rather more cleanly dressed than in the other rooms. Among the visitors were two ladies. One, in mourning, poorly dressed, was sitting at the table opposite the chief clerk and writing something at his dictation. The other lady, very stout and purple-red, with blotches, a striking woman, and somehow very gorgeously dressed, with a brooch on her bosom the size of a saucer, stood to one side waiting for something. Raskolnikov thrust his summons at the chief clerk. He glanced at it in passing, said, “Wait,” and went on attending to the lady in mourning.
He breathed more freely. “It can’t be that!” Little by little he began to take heart; he urged himself with all his strength to take heart and collect himself.
“Some stupidity, some tiny carelessness, and I can give myself away completely! Hm... a pity there is no air here,” he added, “it is stifling... My head is spinning even more... and my mind too...”

He felt a terrible disorder in his whole being. He was afraid he would not be able to control himself. He tried to fasten on something and think about anything at all, something completely unrelated, but he could not manage it at all. The chief clerk, however, interested him greatly: he kept wanting to guess something from his face, to see through him. He was a very young man, about twenty-two, with a dark and mobile face that looked older than his years, dressed in the fashion and like a dandy, with his hair parted at the back, combed and pomaded, with a great many rings on his white fingers, scrubbed with brushes, and gold chains on his waistcoat. With a foreigner who was there he even exchanged a few words in French, and very creditably.
“Luiza Ivanovna, you should sit down,” he said in passing to the gorgeously dressed purple-red lady, who was still standing as if not daring to sit down herself, though there was a chair beside her.

“Ich danke,” she said, and quietly, with a rustle of silk, sank onto the chair. Her pale-blue dress with white lace trimming spread around the chair like a balloon and took up almost half the room. There was a waft of perfume. But the lady was evidently timid about taking up half the room and smelling so strongly of perfume, though she smiled in a way that was cowardly and brazen at once, but with evident uneasiness.

The lady in mourning finished at last and began to get up. Suddenly, with some noise, very dashingly and with a special swing of the shoulders at every step, an officer came in, threw his cap with its cockade on the table and sat down in an armchair. The gorgeous lady positively jumped up from her seat when she saw him, and began curtseying with a kind of special rapture; but the officer paid not the slightest attention to her, and she no longer dared sit down in his presence. He was a lieutenant, the assistant district superintendent, with reddish moustaches sticking out horizontally on both sides, and with extremely small features, which expressed nothing in particular, however, except a certain insolence. He looked sideways at Raskolnikov, and partly with indignation: his clothes were really too wretched, and, in spite of all his humiliation, his bearing still did not match his clothes; Raskolnikov, carelessly, looked at him too straight and too long, so that he even took offence.
“What do you want?” he shouted, probably surprised that such a ragamuffin had no thought of shrinking away from his lightning glance.
“I was summoned... by a summons...” Raskolnikov answered somehow.

“It’s the case of recovering money from him, from the student,” the chief clerk hurried to say, tearing himself away from his papers. “Here!” And he tossed Raskolnikov a notebook, pointing to a place in it. “Read it!”
“Money? What money?” thought Raskolnikov. “But... then it certainly isn’t that!” And he started with joy. He suddenly felt terribly, inexpressibly light. Everything fell from his shoulders.
“And what time were you told to come, my dear sir?” shouted the lieutenant, more and more offended at heaven knows what. “You are told nine, and now it’s past eleven!”

“It was only brought to me a quarter of an hour ago,” Raskolnikov answered loudly, over his shoulder, he too suddenly and unexpectedly angry, and even finding a certain pleasure in it. “It is enough that I have come at all, ill with a fever.”
“Kindly do not shout!”
“I am not shouting, I am speaking very evenly; it is you who are shouting at me; and I am a student and I will not allow anyone to shout at me.”
The assistant flared up so much that at first he could not even utter a word, and only some spray flew from his lips. He jumped up from his seat.
“Kindly be si-i-ilent! You are in a government office. No r-r-rudeness, sir!”

“And you are in a government office too,” cried Raskolnikov, “and besides shouting, you are smoking a cigarette, so you are showing disrespect to all of us.” Having said this, Raskolnikov felt an inexpressible pleasure.
The chief clerk looked at them with a smile. The hot-tempered lieutenant was evidently taken aback.

“That is none of your business, sir!” he shouted at last, somehow unnaturally loudly. “But kindly give the declaration that is required of you. Show him, Alexander Grigoryevich. There are complaints against you! You don’t pay your debts! What a fine falcon has flown in!”
But Raskolnikov was no longer listening, and greedily seized the paper, looking for the answer to the riddle as fast as he could. He read it once, twice, and did not understand.
“What is this?” he asked the chief clerk.

“It is a demand for money from you on a promissory note, a recovery. You must either pay with all costs, fines and so on, or give a written declaration of when you can pay, and at the same time an undertaking not to leave the capital until you have paid, and not to sell or conceal your property. And the creditor is free to sell your property and to proceed against you according to the law.”
“But I... don’t owe anyone anything!”

“That is not our business. Here we have received for recovery an overdue and legally protested promissory note for a hundred and fifteen roubles, issued by you to the widow of a collegiate assessor, Zarnitsyna, nine months ago, and passed by the widow Zarnitsyna in payment to Court Councillor Chebarov, and so we summon you to make a declaration.”
“But she is my landlady!”
“Well, what if she is your landlady?”

The chief clerk looked at him with a condescending smile of pity and at the same time of a certain triumph, as at a novice who is just beginning to come under fire: “Well, how do you feel now?” But what, what did he care now about a promissory note, about recovery! Was it worth the slightest anxiety now, or even the slightest attention! He stood, read, listened, answered, even asked questions himself, but all mechanically. The triumph of self-preservation, deliverance from the danger that had been crushing him: that was what filled his whole being at that moment, without foresight, without analysis, without future guessing and riddling, without doubts and without questions. It was a minute of complete, immediate, purely animal joy. But at that very minute something like thunder and lightning broke out in the office. The lieutenant, still shaken by the disrespect, all aflame, and evidently wishing to restore his injured pride, fell with all his thunderbolts on the unhappy “gorgeous lady”, who had been looking at him with the stupidest of smiles ever since he came in.

“And you, you so-and-so,” he suddenly shouted at the top of his voice (the lady in mourning had already gone out), “what happened at your place last night? Eh? Disgrace again, you’re making a row for the whole street to hear. Fighting and drunkenness again. You’re dreaming of the house of correction! Didn’t I tell you, didn’t I warn you ten times that I wouldn’t let it pass the eleventh time? And here you are again, again, you so-and-so!”

The paper even fell out of Raskolnikov’s hands, and he stared wildly at the gorgeous lady who was being dressed down so unceremoniously; but soon he grasped what it was about, and at once the whole story began to please him very much indeed. He listened with pleasure, so much that he wanted to laugh, laugh, laugh... All his nerves were jumping.
“Ilya Petrovich!” the chief clerk began solicitously, but stopped to bide his time, because there was no holding back the boiling lieutenant except by the arms, as he knew from his own experience.

As for the gorgeous lady, at first she positively trembled at the thunder and lightning; but, strange to say, the more numerous and stronger the abuse became, the more amiable her look grew, the more charming the smile she turned on the formidable lieutenant. She shuffled on the spot and curtseyed incessantly, waiting impatiently to be allowed at last to put in a word of her own, and her chance came.

“No noise and no fight vas at my place, Herr Kapitän,” she suddenly rattled off, as if a bag of peas had been spilt, with a strong German accent, though in brisk Russian, “and no, no scandal, but zey come drunk, and I vill tell it all, Herr Kapitän, and I am not guilty... I have a noble house, Herr Kapitän, and noble manners, Herr Kapitän, and I alvays, alvays myself vanted no scandal. But zey come quite drunk and zen ask for three bottles more, and zen one lift up his feet and begin to play ze piano viz his foot, and zat is not at all nice in a noble house, and he ganz break ze piano, and zere is no, no manners at all here, and I said so. And he take ze bottle and begin to push everyone from behind viz ze bottle. And zen I quick call ze caretaker and Karl come, and he take Karl and hit him in ze eye, and Henriette he hit in ze eye too, and me he hit on ze cheek five times. And zat is so indelicate in a noble house, Herr Kapitän, and I scream. And he open ze window on ze canal and stand in ze window and squeal like a little pig; and zat is a shame. And how can one squeal in ze window on ze street like a little pig; and zat is a shame. Fui-fui-fui! And Karl pull him from behind by his coat from ze window, and zen, it is true, Herr Kapitän, he tear his coat. And zen he shout zat man muss pay him fifteen roubles fine. And I myself, Herr Kapitän, pay him five roubles for his coat. And zat is not a noble guest, Herr Kapitän, and he make every kind of scandal! I, he said, vill print a big satire about you, because I can write everything about you in all ze newspapers.”
“One of the writing fraternity, then?”
“Yes, Herr Kapitän, and vat a not noble guest it is, Herr Kapitän, ven in a noble house...”
“Now, now, now! Enough! I have told you, told you, I told you...”
“Ilya Petrovich!” the chief clerk said again significantly. The lieutenant glanced at him quickly; the chief clerk nodded his head slightly.

“...So here is my last word to you, most respected Laviza Ivanovna, and it is for the last time,” the lieutenant went on. “If there is a scandal in your noble house even one more time, I will haul you up before the court myself, as they say in high style. Do you hear? So a literary man, a writer, took five roubles in a ‘noble house’ for his coat-tails? There they are, your writers!” And he cast a contemptuous look at Raskolnikov. “The day before yesterday there was a scene in a tavern too: one of them dined and then wouldn’t pay; ‘I’ll describe you in a satire for that,’ he says. On a steamer last week another one called the respectable family of a civil councillor, his wife and daughter, the vilest names. The other day one was thrown out of a confectioner’s by the scruff of his neck. That’s what they are like, writers, literary men, students, heralds... pah! And you, be off with you! I’ll look in on you myself... then look out! Do you hear?”

Luiza Ivanovna, with hasty amiability, began curtseying in all directions, and, curtseying, backed to the door; but in the doorway she bumped backwards into a fine-looking officer with an open, fresh face and superb, very thick fair side-whiskers. This was Nikodim Fomich himself, the district superintendent. Luiza Ivanovna hastened to curtsey almost to the floor and, with quick little steps, hopping, flew out of the office.

“Thunder again, thunder and lightning again, a waterspout, a hurricane!” Nikodim Fomich said amiably and in a friendly way to Ilya Petrovich. “Your heart has been stirred up again, you’ve boiled over again! I heard you from the stairs.”

“Oh, vot!” Ilya Petrovich said with gentlemanly nonchalance (and not even ‘what’, but somehow ‘Oh, va-at!’), moving to another table with some papers and picturesquely jerking his shoulders at every step, wherever the step went, there went the shoulder. “Here, sir, if you please: the gentleman is a writer, I mean a student, a former one, that is; he doesn’t pay his debts, he has given bills, he won’t clear out of his lodging, there are constant complaints against him, and he was pleased to take offence because I lit a cigarette in his presence! They behave like s-s-scoundrels themselves, and here, sir, look at him: there he is now in all his most attractive glory, sir!”

“Poverty is no vice, my friend, but there it is! We know, he’s gunpowder, he couldn’t stand an insult. You must have taken offence at something against him, and you couldn’t hold yourself back,” Nikodim Fomich went on, turning amiably to Raskolnikov. “But you were wrong there: he is the mo-o-ost no-o-oble of men, I tell you, but gunpowder, gunpowder! He flares up, boils over, burns out, and that’s all! It’s all over! And all that’s left is a heart of gold! In the regiment they used to call him ‘Lieutenant Gunpowder’...”
“And what a r-r-regiment it was!” exclaimed Ilya Petrovich, very pleased to be tickled so pleasantly, but still sulking.
Raskolnikov suddenly wanted to say something extraordinarily pleasant to them all.

“But really, Captain,” he began very casually, turning suddenly to Nikodim Fomich, “consider my position too... I am even ready to ask his pardon, if I have been at all disrespectful on my side. I am a poor and sick student, weighed down” (he actually said “weighed down”) “by poverty. I am a former student because I cannot keep myself now, but I shall be getting money... I have a mother and sister in X. province. They will send me some, and I... shall pay. My landlady is a good woman, but she is so angry that I have lost my lessons and haven’t paid for four months that she doesn’t even send up my dinner... And I don’t understand at all what this bill is! Now she is demanding payment from me on this promissory note; how am I to pay her, judge for yourselves!..”
“But that is not our business...” the chief clerk was about to remark again...

“Allow me, allow me, I entirely agree with you, but allow me to explain too,” Raskolnikov took it up again, addressing not the chief clerk but still Nikodim Fomich, but trying with all his might to address Ilya Petrovich too, though the latter stubbornly pretended to be rummaging in his papers and contemptuously paid no attention to him. “Allow me on my side to explain that I have been living with her for about three years now, ever since I came from the provinces, and before... before... but why should I not confess in my turn: from the very beginning I gave a promise that I would marry her daughter, a verbal promise, quite freely given... She was a girl... in fact I even liked her... though I was not in love... in a word, youth, that is, I mean to say that my landlady gave me a lot of credit then, and I led a sort of life... I was very frivolous...”

“Nobody is asking you for such intimacies, my dear sir, and there is no time either,” Ilya Petrovich interrupted rudely and triumphantly; but Raskolnikov stopped him hotly, though it had suddenly become extremely hard for him to speak.

“But allow me, allow me to tell it all, in part... how it happened and... in my turn... although it is unnecessary, I agree with you, to tell it... but a year ago this girl died of typhus, and I stayed on as a lodger, as before, and my landlady, when she moved to her present flat, said to me... and said it in a friendly way... that she trusted me completely and all that... but would I not give her this promissory note for a hundred and fifteen roubles, all that she reckoned I owed her? Allow me: she said precisely that, as soon as I gave her this paper, she would give me credit again as much as I liked, and that never, never, for her part (those were her own words), would she make use of this paper until I paid myself... And now, when I have lost my lessons and have nothing to eat, she puts it in for recovery... What am I to say now?”

“All these touching details, my dear sir, are no concern of ours,” Ilya Petrovich cut him short insolently. “You must give a declaration and an undertaking, and whether you were pleased to be in love and all those tragic passages are no business of ours at all.”
“Well, now you are... being cruel...” muttered Nikodim Fomich, sitting down at the table and beginning to sign papers too. He felt somehow ashamed.
“Write, then,” the chief clerk said to Raskolnikov.
“Write what?” he asked, somehow especially rudely.
“I will dictate it to you.”

It seemed to Raskolnikov that the chief clerk had become more offhand and more contemptuous with him after his confession; but, strange to say, he himself suddenly did not care in the least about anyone’s opinion, and this change happened somehow in a moment, in a single minute. If he had wanted to think a little, he would certainly have been surprised at how he could have talked to them like that a minute before, and even forced his feelings on them. And where had those feelings come from? On the contrary, now, if the room had suddenly been filled not with police officers but with his very best friends, even then, it seems, he would not have found a single human word for them, so empty had his heart suddenly become. A gloomy sensation of tormenting, endless solitude and estrangement suddenly made itself consciously felt in his soul. It was not the baseness of his heartfelt outpourings before Ilya Petrovich, nor the baseness of the lieutenant’s triumph over him, that had suddenly turned his heart over like this. Oh, what did he care now about his own baseness, about all these vanities, lieutenants, German women, recoveries, offices and so on, and so on! If he had been sentenced to be burned at that moment, even then he would not have stirred, and would hardly even have listened attentively to the sentence. Something was happening to him that was completely unknown to him, new, sudden, and that had never been before. It was not that he understood it, but he felt clearly, with the whole force of feeling, that not only with sentimental effusions, as just now, but with anything at all, he could no longer turn to these people in the police office, and that even if they had all been his own brothers and sisters and not police lieutenants, even then there would be no reason whatever for him to turn to them, in any circumstance of life; he had never until that moment experienced such a strange and terrible sensation. And what was most tormenting of all: it was more a sensation than an awareness, than an idea; an immediate sensation, the most tormenting of all the sensations he had lived through in his life until then.

The chief clerk began dictating to him the form of declaration usual in such cases, that is, I cannot pay, I promise to pay on such and such a date (some time), I will not leave the town, I will not sell or give away my property, and so on.
“But you can’t write, the pen is falling out of your hand,” the chief clerk remarked, looking at Raskolnikov with curiosity. “Are you ill?”
“Yes... my head is spinning... go on!”
“That’s all! Sign it.”
The chief clerk took back the paper and turned to the others.

Raskolnikov gave back the pen, but instead of getting up and going away, he put both elbows on the table and squeezed his head in his hands. It was as if a nail were being driven into the crown of his head. A strange thought suddenly came to him: to get up now, go to Nikodim Fomich and tell him everything about yesterday, everything to the last detail, then go with them to his lodging and show them the things in the corner, in the hole. The urge was so strong that he had already risen from his seat to carry it out. “Shouldn’t I think it over for a minute at least?” flashed through his head. “No, better without thinking, and get it off my shoulders!” But suddenly he stopped as if rooted to the spot: Nikodim Fomich was speaking hotly to Ilya Petrovich, and the words reached him:

“It can’t be, they’ll both be released! In the first place, everything contradicts it; judge for yourself: why would they call the caretaker if it was their doing? To inform on themselves? Or as a trick? No, that would be too cunning! And finally, the student Pestryakov was seen right at the gate by both caretakers and a tradeswoman at the very moment he went in: he was walking with three friends and parted from them right at the gate, and asked the caretakers about lodgings, while his friends were still there. Now, would a man ask about lodgings if he had come with such an intention? And as for Koch, before going to the old woman he sat for half an hour downstairs at the silversmith’s, and went up from him to the old woman at exactly a quarter to eight. Now consider...”

“But wait, how did they come to contradict themselves like that: they assert themselves that they knocked and that the door was locked, and three minutes later, when they came with the caretaker, it turns out that the door was open?”

“That’s just the point: the murderer must have been sitting in there and had bolted the door; and they would certainly have caught him there if Koch hadn’t been a fool and gone for the caretaker himself. It was precisely in that interval that he managed to get down the stairs and slip past them somehow. Koch crosses himself with both hands: ‘If I had stayed there,’ he says, ‘he would have jumped out and killed me with the axe.’ He wants to have a thanksgiving service said, he-he!..”
“And nobody saw the murderer?”
“Why, how could anybody see him there? The house is a Noah’s ark,” remarked the chief clerk, who had been listening from his place.
“The thing is clear, the thing is clear!” Nikodim Fomich repeated hotly.
“No, the thing is very unclear,” Ilya Petrovich clinched it.
Raskolnikov picked up his hat and went towards the door, but he did not reach the door...

When he came to, he saw that he was sitting on a chair, that some man was supporting him on the right, that on the left stood another man with a yellow glass filled with yellow water, and that Nikodim Fomich was standing in front of him and looking at him intently; he got up from the chair.
“What is this, are you ill?” Nikodim Fomich asked rather sharply.
“Even when he was signing, he could hardly move the pen,” remarked the chief clerk, sitting down in his place and turning to his papers again.

“And have you been ill long?” Ilya Petrovich shouted from his place, also sorting papers. He too, of course, had been looking at the sick man while he was in his faint, but he had moved away at once when he came to.
“Since yesterday...” Raskolnikov muttered in reply.
“And did you go out yesterday?”
“I did.”
“Ill?”
“Ill.”
“At what time?”
“After seven in the evening.”
“And where, may I ask?”
“Along the street.”
“Short and clear.”
Raskolnikov answered sharply, abruptly, as white as a handkerchief, and without lowering his black, inflamed eyes before Ilya Petrovich’s look.
“He can hardly stand on his feet, and you...” Nikodim Fomich was about to remark.

“No mat-ter!” Ilya Petrovich said somehow peculiarly. Nikodim Fomich was about to add something more, but, glancing at the chief clerk, who was also looking at him very intently, he fell silent. Everyone suddenly fell silent. It was strange.
“Well, sir, very good, sir,” Ilya Petrovich concluded. “We are not detaining you.”

Raskolnikov went out. He could still hear how, after he had gone, a lively conversation began, in which the questioning voice of Nikodim Fomich sounded most clearly of all... In the street he came fully to himself.
“A search, a search, a search right away!” he repeated to himself, hurrying to get home. “The robbers! They suspect!” The fear of before seized him again, all over, from head to foot.
## CHAPTER VII

In the middle of the street stood a carriage, smart and fit for a gentleman, drawn by a pair of spirited grey horses; there were no passengers, and the coachman himself had got down from the box and was standing beside it; the horses were being held by the bridles. A great crowd of people pressed around, with the police in front of them all. One of them had a lighted lantern in his hand, with which, bending down, he was lighting up something on the roadway, right by the wheels. Everyone was talking, shouting, gasping; the coachman seemed bewildered and kept repeating now and then:
“What a sin! Lord, what a sin!”

Raskolnikov pushed his way through as far as he could, and at last saw the object of all this bustle and curiosity. On the ground lay a man who had just been run down by the horses, unconscious by the look of it, very badly dressed, but in “gentleman’s” clothes, all covered in blood. Blood was flowing from his face, from his head; his face was all battered, scraped and mangled. It was clear that he had been run over in earnest.

“Good Lord!” the coachman lamented. “How could I have seen him in time! If I had been driving fast, or hadn’t shouted to him; but I was driving not in a hurry, steady. Everyone saw it: people may lie, but not me. A drunk man won’t light a candle to God, that’s well known!.. I see him, he’s crossing the street, staggering, nearly falling; I shouted once, and again, and a third time, and held the horses in; and he fell straight under their feet! Whether he did it on purpose, or he was very far gone... The horses are young, skittish; they pulled, and he cried out, and they pulled worse... and there’s the trouble.”
“That’s just how it was!” came a witness’s voice from the crowd.
“He shouted, it’s true, he shouted to him three times,” said another voice.
“Exactly three times, everybody heard!” cried a third.

The coachman, however, was not very downcast or frightened. It was evident that the carriage belonged to a rich and important owner who was waiting for its arrival somewhere; the police, of course, were very concerned about how to settle this last circumstance. The injured man had to be taken to the police station and the hospital. No one knew his name.
Meanwhile Raskolnikov had pushed his way through and bent down still closer. Suddenly the lantern lit up the unhappy man’s face brightly; he recognised him.

“I know him, I know him!” he shouted, squeezing right to the front. “He’s an official, retired, a titular councillor, Marmeladov! He lives here, near by, in Kozel’s house... A doctor, quickly! I’ll pay, look!” He pulled money out of his pocket and showed it to a policeman. He was in amazing agitation.

The police were glad to have found out who the injured man was. Raskolnikov gave his own name too, gave his address, and with all his might, as if it were his own father, urged them to carry the unconscious Marmeladov to his lodging as quickly as possible.

“Here, three houses along,” he fussed, “Kozel’s house, a German, a rich one... He was probably drunk just now, making his way home. I know him... He’s a drunkard... He has a family there, a wife, children, a daughter. It will take time to drag him to the hospital, and there’s sure to be a doctor in the house! I’ll pay, I’ll pay!.. At least he’ll have his own people to look after him, they’ll help him at once, or else he’ll die before he gets to the hospital...”

He even managed to slip something unnoticed into a hand; the matter, however, was clear and lawful, and in any case help was nearer here. The injured man was lifted and carried; helpers were found. Kozel’s house was about thirty paces away. Raskolnikov walked behind, carefully holding up the head and showing the way.
“This way, this way! On the stairs you must carry him head first; turn him round... that’s it! I’ll pay, I’ll thank you,” he muttered.

Katerina Ivanovna, as always as soon as she had a free minute, had at once begun walking up and down her little room, from the window to the stove and back, her arms tightly folded across her breast, talking to herself and coughing. Lately she had begun to talk more and more often with her eldest girl, ten-year-old Polenka, who, though there was still much she did not understand, had understood very well that her mother needed her, and so she always followed her with her big, clever eyes and tried with all her might to pretend that she understood everything. This time Polenka was undressing her little brother, who had been unwell all day, to put him to bed. While waiting for his shirt to be changed (it was to be washed that same night), the boy sat on a chair in silence, with a serious face, upright and motionless, his little legs stretched out in front of him, pressed tightly together, heels towards the company and toes turned out. He was listening to what Mama was saying to his sister, pouting his lips, his eyes wide open and not moving, exactly as all clever little boys are supposed to sit when they are being undressed to go to bed. A girl still smaller than he, in utter rags, stood by the screen waiting her turn. The door onto the stairs was open, to give some protection at least against the waves of tobacco smoke that burst in from the other rooms and kept making the poor consumptive cough long and painfully. Katerina Ivanovna seemed to have grown even thinner that week, and the red spots on her cheeks burned brighter than before.

“You wouldn’t believe, you can’t even imagine, Polenka,” she was saying as she walked about the room, “how gaily and grandly we lived in Papa’s house, and how this drunkard has ruined me and will ruin you all! Papa was a colonel in the civil service and very nearly a governor; he had only one more step to take, so that everyone came to see him and said: ‘We already regard you, Ivan Mikhailych, as our governor.’ When I... khe! when I... khe-khe-khe... oh, accursed life!” she cried, coughing up phlegm and clutching her chest. “When I... ah, when at the last ball... at the marshal of nobility’s... Princess Bezzemelnaya saw me (she who gave me her blessing afterwards, when I married your papa, Polya), she asked at once: ‘Isn’t that the charming girl who danced the shawl dance at the leaving ceremony?’...
